text: Contoso Skateboard Store is developing Power BI reports for its sales division. You are tasked with designing a report for the business analyst team. What is the most appropriate design approach for this audience?

options.text: A. Provide high-level KPIs with minimal interactivity
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Providing high-level KPIs with minimal interactivity is not the most appropriate design approach for the business analyst team. Business analysts typically require detailed data and the ability to interact with the data to gain insights and make informed decisions.

options.text: B. Include detailed data with slicers, filters, and drill-through capabilities
options.explanation: Including detailed data with slicers, filters, and drill-through capabilities is the most appropriate design approach for the business analyst team. This approach allows analysts to explore the data, filter it based on specific criteria, and drill down into details to uncover trends and patterns.

options.text: C. Focus on operational metrics and raw data exports
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Focusing on operational metrics and raw data exports may not be the best design approach for the business analyst team. While operational metrics are important, analysts also need the ability to analyze and visualize data in a more interactive and dynamic manner.

options.text: D. Limit visuals to static charts and avoid user-driven exploration
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Limiting visuals to static charts and avoiding user-driven exploration is not ideal for the business analyst team. Business analysts require the flexibility to explore data, create custom views, and derive insights from the data through interactive features like drill-downs and filters.

explanation: Correct Answer B. Include detailed data with slicers, filters, and drill-through capabilities Why Correct Analysts need to explore data deeply to evaluate strategies, identify trends, and recommend changes. Interactive features like slicers and drill-throughs empower them to perform ad hoc analysis and uncover insights. Why Others Are Wrong A. High-level KPIs are more suitable for executives, not analysts. C. Operational metrics and raw exports are better suited for information workers. D. Static visuals limit exploration, which contradicts the analyst’s need for flexibility. Keep in Mind: Analysts require flexible, interactive reports for deep data exploration Drill-through pages help uncover granular insights Slicers and filters allow dynamic segmentation of data Analysts often compare trends, performance, and strategy effectiveness Reports should support hypothesis testing and scenario analysis Include calculated measures and DAX logic to support complex queries Use tables, matrix visuals, and charts that allow sorting and filtering Provide access to historical data for trend analysis Avoid oversimplification-analysts prefer depth over brevity Validate report logic with the analyst team before publishing References: Identify the audience - Training | Microsoft Learn

An operational report is best for an inventory report with interactive features like a Submit Order button. explanation: Correct Answer A - 4 B - 1 C - 2 D - 3 Why Correct Each report type is designed for a specific purpose: Dashboards summarize performance for executives Analytical reports support deep exploration Operational reports enable daily decisions and actions Educational reports guide unfamiliar users through data Why Others Are Wrong Misaligning report types with use cases leads to poor user experience and ineffective reporting. For example, using an analytical report for executives adds unnecessary complexity. Keep in Mind: Analytical reports answer “Why did that happen?” Operational reports support real-time decisions Educational reports explain unfamiliar topics Dashboards are strategic, not exploratory Match report type to user role and task Use interactivity only where needed Avoid mixing report types unless justified Validate with stakeholders before finalizing Consider UX and navigation flow Use visuals that match the report’s purpose Exam Tips: Memorize report type definitions and goals Match report types to business scenarios Know which features belong to each report type Expect match-the-pair questions in the exam Practice identifying report types from descriptions References: Determine report types - Training | Microsoft Learn

text: Contoso Skateboard Store is rolling out a Power BI report for warehouse workers who use mobile phones and augmented reality headsets during inventory checks. What is the most appropriate design adjustment to ensure usability across smaller form factors?

options.text: A. Retain all visuals and layout from the desktop version to ensure consistency
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Retaining all visuals and layout from the desktop version may result in a cluttered and difficult-to-navigate report on smaller form factors like mobile phones and augmented reality headsets. It is important to optimize the design for the specific needs and limitations of these devices.

options.text: B. Refactor the report to include fewer, larger visuals optimized for portrait orientation
options.explanation: Refactoring the report to include fewer, larger visuals optimized for portrait orientation is the most appropriate adjustment to ensure usability across smaller form factors. This design approach allows for better visibility and interaction on mobile devices, making it easier for warehouse workers to access and interpret the information.

options.text: C. Add more slicers and filters to enhance interactivity on mobile devices
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Adding more slicers and filters may enhance interactivity on mobile devices, but it may not address the primary issue of optimizing the report for smaller form factors. While interactivity is important, the focus should be on redesigning the visuals and layout to improve usability on mobile phones and augmented reality headsets.

options.text: D. Replace visuals with detailed tables to maximize data visibility on small screens
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Replacing visuals with detailed tables to maximize data visibility on small screens may not be the best approach for warehouse workers using mobile phones and augmented reality headsets. Tables can be difficult to read and navigate on smaller devices, and a focus on larger, optimized visuals would likely provide a better user experience.

explanation: Correct Answer B. Refactor the report to include fewer, larger visuals optimized for portrait orientation Why Correct Smaller form factors like phones and AR headsets require simplified layouts with fewer visuals that are large enough for easy viewing and interaction. text: You are designing a Power BI report for Contoso Skateboard Store with accessibility in mind. Which of the following practices support accessibility requirements for report consumers with low vision or physical disabilities? (Select all that apply)

options.explanation: Using clear and large-sized fonts improves readability for users with low vision or visual impairments, making it easier for them to consume the information presented in the report.

options.text: B. Add alt text to visuals to support screen readers
options.explanation: Adding alt text to visuals allows screen readers to describe the content of the visuals to users who are visually impaired or blind, ensuring they can understand the information conveyed in the report.

options.text: E. Apply clear and distinctive contrasting colors

options.text: F. Rely solely on mouse hover interactions for tooltips and navigation

options.text: C. UX is only relevant for mobile users UI applies to all devices

text: Contoso Ltd. is preparing a Power BI solution and wants to ensure analysts understand accessibility standards. The BI team asks: Which user interface requirement is an example of an accessibility requirement?

options.text: Augmented reality
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Augmented reality is not an example of an accessibility requirement in the user interface. It is a technology that enhances the user experience but does not specifically address accessibility needs for users with disabilities.

options.text: Contrasting colors
options.explanation: Contrasting colors are an example of an accessibility requirement as they help users with visual impairments distinguish between different elements on the screen. High contrast between foreground and background colors can improve readability and usability for all users. Few other Power BI accessibility features Alt text: This is short text you add to visuals (like charts or images) so that screen readers can describe them to users who cannot see the visuals clearly. Keyboard navigation: Power BI supports moving through reports using only the keyboard, which helps users who cannot use a mouse. Screen reader support: Screen readers can read out the content of reports, including titles, filters, and data points, so people with low or no vision can still understand the report. Accessible visuals: Choosing visuals that are easy to interpret (like bar charts instead of complex custom visuals) makes reports clearer for everyone. High contrast mode: Power BI can switch to high contrast mode so text and visuals stand out more, helping users with vision difficulties. In short, accessibility in Power BI is about making sure everyone can read, understand, and interact with reports, no matter their abilities.

options.text: Organizational colors
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Organizational colors are not necessarily related to accessibility requirements. While consistent use of colors can improve brand recognition and user experience, it does not directly address accessibility needs for users with disabilities.

options.text: Portrait orientation
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Portrait orientation is not an example of an accessibility requirement in the user interface. It is a design choice that may impact the layout and presentation of content but does not specifically address accessibility needs for users with disabilities.

explanation: Contrasting colors is an accessibility requirement and helps report consumers with low or no vision to distinguish different colors. Keep in Mind: Contrasting colors means using colors that are very different from each other, like black text on a white background. This is called an accessibility requirement because it makes reports easier to read for people who have trouble seeing or telling colors apart. In Power BI, contrasting colors in charts and visuals help report consumers with low vision or color blindness clearly see differences between data points. For example, if a chart uses light green and dark green side by side, some people may not notice the difference. But if you use green and orange, the contrast makes it clear. References: Check your knowledge - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A client of Contoso Ltd. is building a reporting solution and wants to ensure the report layout is intuitive. She asks: Which of the following best describes effective placement of report objects for an audience that reads left to right (LTR)?

options.text: Place the most important information in the upper-right corner and arrange elements from right to left.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Placing the most important information in the upper-right corner and arranging elements from right to left may cause confusion for an audience that reads left to right. This placement may disrupt the natural flow of reading and make it difficult for viewers to quickly grasp the key insights of the report.

options.text: Center all report objects and avoid grouping related items.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Centering all report objects and avoiding grouping related items may lead to a lack of visual hierarchy and organization. This approach can make it challenging for viewers to prioritize information and understand the relationships between different elements in the report.

options.text: Place the most important information in the upper-left corner and arrange elements from left to right and top to bottom.
options.explanation: Placing the most important information in the upper-left corner and arranging elements from left to right and top to bottom aligns with the natural reading pattern of an audience that reads left to right. This placement allows viewers to easily scan and digest the content in a logical sequence, enhancing the overall readability and comprehension of the report.

options.text: Randomly distribute report objects to create visual interest.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Randomly distributing report objects to create visual interest may result in a cluttered and chaotic layout that hinders the audience's ability to navigate the information effectively. This approach can make it challenging for viewers to focus on the key insights and may lead to confusion and disengagement.

explanation: Good placement of report objects contributes to an ordered report design. Generally, you should place the most important information in the upper-left corner of the page and arrange the report elements from left to right and top to bottom. FAQ: 1. Why is placement important in report design? Proper placement ensures that information is easy to read, visually appealing, and logically organized. It helps users quickly find and understand key insights. 2. Where should the most important information be placed? For left-to-right (LTR) readers (e.g., English): Upper-left corner. For right-to-left (RTL) readers (e.g., Arabic, Hebrew): Upper-right corner. 3. What is the recommended reading flow for report elements? LTR audiences: Arrange elements from left to right and top to bottom. 4. How should report objects be aligned? Align objects vertically and horizontally to create a clean, ordered layout. Misaligned elements can appear cluttered or unprofessional. 5. Should related report objects be grouped? Yes. Grouping related elements helps users understand relationships between data and improves overall readability. 6. What is the rule of thirds, and how does it apply? The rule of thirds divides a page into a 3x3 grid. Placing key elements along the lines or intersections of this grid enhances visual balance and focus. 7. Is centering all objects a good practice? Not always. While centering can work in some cases, it often lacks the structure and energy of a well-aligned, grid-based layout. 8. How does placement affect user engagement? A well-placed layout draws attention, reduces cognitive load, and keeps users engaged with the content. 9. Can poor placement impact data interpretation? Absolutely. Disorganized or random placement can confuse users, obscure insights, and reduce the effectiveness of the report. 10. Are there tools to help with placement in Power BI or Power Apps? Yes. Tools like snap-to-grid, alignment guides, and grouping features help maintain consistent and professional layouts.

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer wants to summarize key metrics in paragraph form and ensure the values update dynamically when filters are applied. Which of the following statements are true about this approach? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. A text box can embed dynamic values from the semantic model
options.explanation: A text box in Power BI can indeed embed dynamic values from the semantic model, allowing the report designer to display key metrics in paragraph form that update dynamically when filters are applied. This provides flexibility in presenting data in a narrative format.

options.text: B. Smart narrative visual automatically generates text-based insights
options.explanation: The Smart narrative visual in Power BI automatically generates text-based insights based on the data in the report. This feature is useful for summarizing key metrics in paragraph form and ensuring that the values update dynamically when filters are applied, making it a suitable option for the report designer's requirements.

options.text: C. Dynamic values in a text box do not respond to page filters
options.explanation: Dynamic values in a text box in Power BI can respond to page filters, allowing the values to update dynamically based on the selected filters. This feature enhances the interactivity and flexibility of the report, providing users with real-time insights based on their selections.

options.text: D. You can format dynamic values inside a text box
options.explanation: Power BI allows for formatting dynamic values inside a text box, giving the report designer the ability to customize the appearance of the key metrics being summarized in paragraph form. This feature enhances the visual presentation of the data and improves readability for users.

options.text: E. You must use Smart narrative visual to insert dynamic values
options.explanation: While the Smart narrative visual in Power BI is a useful tool for generating text-based insights, it is not the only option for inserting dynamic values in a report. A text box can also be used to display dynamic values from the semantic model, providing the report designer with flexibility in how they present key metrics in paragraph form. The Smart Narrative visual is one option that automatically generates text summaries with dynamic values from visuals. However, you can also insert dynamic values using cards, measures, tooltips, or custom DAX expressions. Smart Narrative is helpful for autogenerated explanations, but it’s not the only way to display dynamic values.

explanation: What is a text box used for? To add formatted text and embed dynamic values from the semantic model. Do dynamic values in a text box respond to filters? Yes. They update automatically based on page-level filters. What is the Smart narrative visual? A visual that automatically generates text summaries and insights from the data. Can you format dynamic values in a text box? Yes. You can apply font styles, colors, and paragraph alignment. Is the text box considered a visual? Technically no, but it behaves like one when dynamic values are embedded. Exam Tips: Know how to embed dynamic values using Q&A Understand the difference between static and dynamic text Recognize that both text box and Smart narrative can be used to summarize data Expect scenario-based questions involving formatting and filter responsiveness Practice inserting and styling dynamic values in Power BI reports References: Use report objects - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A BI analyst is preparing a quarterly performance report for a retail company. The report features a prominent sales trend chart, supporting KPI cards, and a bar chart to show regional comparisons. The executives want the layout to be organized yet visually appealing. Which design strategy would best satisfy this requirement?

options.text: A. Place all visuals in equal-sized containers and distribute them evenly across the page
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Placing all visuals in equal-sized containers and distributing them evenly across the page may create a balanced layout, but it may lack hierarchy and fail to draw attention to the most important information. It may not effectively highlight the key insights for the executive team.

options.text: B. Use a centered layout with symmetrical spacing and identical visual weights
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Using a centered layout with symmetrical spacing and identical visual weights can create a clean and organized look. However, it may lack visual interest and fail to emphasize the most critical information. It may not effectively guide the executive team's focus to the key insights.

options.text: C. Apply a layout that emphasizes one dominant visual supported by smaller contextual elements
options.explanation: Applying a layout that emphasizes one dominant visual supported by smaller contextual elements can create a structured yet visually engaging design. This approach helps draw attention to the most important information while providing additional context through smaller visuals. It aligns with the executive team's request for a layout that feels structured and visually engaging.

options.text: D. Arrange visuals in a grid with no variation in size or placement
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Arranging visuals in a grid with no variation in size or placement may create a neat and organized appearance. However, it may lack hierarchy and fail to guide the executive team's focus to the most critical insights. It may not effectively communicate the key information in a visually engaging way.

explanation: Correct Answer is C - Using one dominant visual supported by smaller elements creates asymmetrical balance, which adds visual interest while maintaining structure. This approach aligns with principles like the golden ratio, guiding the viewer’s attention naturally across the report. Keep in Mind: 1. What does “balance” mean in report design? Balance refers to how visual weight is distributed across a report page. It creates a sense of stability and structure, making the layout easier to read and more visually appealing. 2. What are the types of balance used in reports? Symmetrical Balance: Equal distribution of elements on both sides of the page. Asymmetrical Balance: Unequal but intentional distribution using contrast, size, or positioning to guide attention. 3. How does the golden ratio apply to report design? The golden ratio helps achieve asymmetrical balance by placing one large visual element to attract attention, supported by smaller visuals that provide context. It’s based on the Fibonacci Sequence and has been used in art and architecture for centuries. 4. Why is asymmetrical balance useful? It creates visual interest and guides the viewer’s eye naturally across the report. It avoids monotony while still maintaining structure. 5. Can symmetrical balance be effective in reports? Yes, especially when a formal or evenly weighted layout is needed. However, it can sometimes feel static or predictable. 6. What happens if a report lacks balance? Poor balance can lead to visual clutter, confusion, and difficulty in interpreting data. It may also reduce user engagement. 7. How do I know if my report is balanced? Check whether the layout feels stable and whether the viewer’s attention flows naturally from key visuals to supporting elements. Use alignment, spacing, and size intentionally. 8. Is balance only about visual size? No. Balance also involves color, contrast, alignment, and grouping. Even small elements can carry visual weight depending on how they’re styled. 9. Should I always use the golden ratio? Not necessarily. It’s a helpful guide, but the best layout depends on your audience, content, and goals. Use it when asymmetrical balance is appropriate. 10. Does balance affect report performance or usability? Yes. A well-balanced report improves readability, reduces cognitive load, and enhances user experience, especially for decision-makers who need to absorb insights quickly. Exam Tips: Understand symmetrical vs asymmetrical balance Know how the golden ratio applies to layout design Recognize how visual weight affects user attention Expect scenario-based questions on layout and UX Practice identifying balanced vs unbalanced report designs References: Design the analytical report layout - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is building a sales dashboard that includes revenue trends, customer satisfaction scores, and product performance metrics. Which design approach best applies the principle of proximity?

options.text: A. Place related visuals close together and separate unrelated groups with intentional spacing
options.explanation: Placing related visuals close together and separating unrelated groups with intentional spacing adheres to the principle of proximity. This design approach helps create visual hierarchy and clearly defines different sections within the sales dashboard, making it easier for stakeholders to identify and understand the information presented.

options.text: B. Distribute all visuals evenly across the page regardless of their relationship
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Distributing all visuals evenly across the page regardless of their relationship does not effectively apply the principle of proximity. This approach can lead to a cluttered and confusing layout, making it difficult for stakeholders to differentiate between different sections and understand the data presented in the sales dashboard.

options.text: C. Randomly place visuals to create a dynamic and engaging layout
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Randomly placing visuals to create a dynamic and engaging layout may not be the best way to apply the principle of proximity in this context. While a dynamic layout can be visually appealing, it can also result in a lack of organization and clarity within the sales dashboard, making it challenging for stakeholders to interpret the data effectively.

options.text: D. Center all visuals to maintain symmetry and avoid grouping
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Centering all visuals to maintain symmetry and avoid grouping does not effectively utilize the principle of proximity. While symmetry can be visually pleasing, it may not help stakeholders distinguish between different sections within the sales dashboard. Placing visuals in a centered manner without considering their relationships can lead to confusion and hinder the overall clarity of the dashboard.

explanation: Why Correct Proximity ensures that related report objects are placed near each other, forming logical visual groupings. Using space to separate unrelated sections improves readability and helps users quickly identify patterns and relationships. Why Others Are Wrong Option B ignores logical grouping, making the report harder to interpret Option C sacrifices clarity for visual energy, leading to confusion Option D avoids grouping altogether, which undermines the structure of the report Proximity In a report layout, proximity is concerned with the nearness of report objects. When a report page consists of multiple groups of related objects, you should use space to visually separate them. In the following report design, notice the top-left section labeled key metrics. Related visuals are placed near one another. They're also purposefully and consistently aligned forming a clear section. Keep in Mind: 1. What is proximity in report design? Proximity refers to the nearness of report objects. It helps users understand which visuals are related by placing them close together. 2. Why is proximity important? It improves readability and clarity by visually grouping related elements and separating unrelated ones. 3. How is proximity applied in a report layout? Related visuals are placed near each other and consistently aligned. Unrelated groups are separated using whitespace or layout divisions. 4. Does proximity affect user navigation? Yes. Proper proximity guides the user’s eye through the report in a logical and intuitive way. 5. Can poor proximity lead to confusion? Absolutely. If related visuals are scattered or unrelated visuals are grouped together, users may misinterpret the data or struggle to find key insights. References: Design the analytical report layout - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: Left Side (Section Type): A. Implied Section B. Explicit Section Right Side (Description): Uses colored shapes and overlays to visually separate aligned visuals Aligns groups of visuals in close proximity, using spacing to suggest grouping

options.explanation: Choice A is correct because an Implied Section uses colored shapes and overlays to visually separate aligned visuals, while an Explicit Section aligns groups of visuals in close proximity, using spacing to suggest grouping.

Choice B is incorrect because it incorrectly matches the description of an Implied Section with aligning groups of visuals in close proximity, using spacing to suggest grouping, which is actually the description of an Explicit Section.

explanation: Implied Section: Relies on spacing and proximity to suggest grouping without visual borders By placing visuals close together (and leaving space around them), people naturally understand they’re related. It’s more subtle, but it guides the viewer’s eye and keeps the page balanced. Explicit Section: Uses background shapes or overlays to clearly define visual groups Think of it like drawing boxes or using colored backgrounds to clearly show which visuals belong together. The shapes act like containers, so the viewer immediately sees: “These charts are one group, those charts are another.” Exam Tips: Know the difference between implied and explicit sectioning Understand how spacing and overlays affect layout clarity References: Design visually appealing reports - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is building a dashboard with multiple visuals, including bar charts, KPI cards, and slicers. The visuals are grouped into performance, customer feedback, and regional data sections. The designer ensures that the edges of visuals are aligned and that spacing between visuals is consistent within each section.  Which design principle is being applied?

options.text: A. Alignment to maintain structure and visual consistency across sections
options.explanation: Alignment is the correct design principle being applied in this scenario. By aligning the edges of visuals and maintaining consistent spacing within each section, the designer is ensuring structural integrity and visual consistency across the dashboard, creating a cohesive and organized layout.

options.text: B. Proximity to group related visuals together
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Proximity is not the design principle being applied in this scenario. While grouping related visuals together is important for visual organization, the focus here is on aligning edges, maintaining consistent spacing, and formatting titles and legends uniformly within each section.

options.text: C. Contrast to highlight differences between sections
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Contrast is not the design principle being applied in this scenario. Contrast is typically used to highlight differences between elements, such as colors or sizes, to draw attention. In this case, the designer is focusing on alignment and consistency within each section, rather than emphasizing differences.

options.text: D. Repetition to reinforce visual patterns
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Repetition is not the design principle being applied in this scenario. Repetition is used to reinforce visual patterns and create a sense of unity throughout the design. While uniform formatting of titles and legends may involve repetition, the primary focus here is on alignment and consistency within each section.

explanation: Correct Answer Option A -Alignment to maintain structure and visual consistency across sections Why Correct Alignment ensures that visuals are properly positioned with consistent spacing and formatting. It applies to both layout structure and internal formatting, such as titles and legends. This creates a clean, professional report that guides user attention effectively. Why Others Are Wrong Option B focuses on grouping, not edge alignment or formatting Option C emphasizes visual differentiation, not layout consistency Option D relates to repeated design elements, not positioning or spacing Keep in Mind: 1. What is alignment in report design? Alignment refers to the consistent positioning of visuals and formatting elements to create a structured and readable layout. 2. Why is alignment important? It improves clarity, reduces visual clutter, and helps users navigate the report efficiently. 3. What elements should be aligned? Visual edges, spacing between visuals, titles, legends, and section layouts. 4. What are implied sections? Groups of visuals aligned in close proximity, separated by spacing to suggest logical grouping without explicit borders. 5. Can poor alignment affect user experience? Yes. Misaligned visuals can confuse users, disrupt flow, and reduce the perceived professionalism of the report. Exam Tips: Understand alignment as a layout principle for structure and clarity Know that alignment applies to both visuals and formatting elements Expect scenario-based questions on layout consistency and UX Practice identifying aligned vs misaligned report designs Recognize how alignment supports implied sections and visual flow References: Design visually appealing reports - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is building a Power BI dashboard for the operations team. They want to include a visual that’s not available in the default Visualizations pane. After exploring, they find a suitable visual and plan to use it across both Power BI Desktop and Power BI Service. Which of the following statements are true in this scenario? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A. The designer can import the visual from Microsoft AppSource
options.explanation: The designer can import custom visuals from Microsoft AppSource, which is a marketplace for various business applications, including Power BI visuals. This allows the designer to easily access and integrate new visuals into their Power BI dashboard. Go through the steps to import from Appsource. Import Power BI visuals from AppSource or from a file - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: B. The designer can upload a PBIVIZ file to add the custom visual
options.explanation: Uploading a PBIVIZ file is another way for the designer to add custom visuals to their Power BI dashboard. Power BI visuals are packaged in .pbiviz files that include code for rendering the data served to them. Anyone can create a custom visual and package it as a single .pbiviz file that can be imported into a Power BI report. Import Power BI visuals from AppSource or from a file - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: C. Custom visuals are only supported in Power BI Desktop
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Custom visuals are not limited to Power BI Desktop; they can also be used in Power BI Service. This allows the designer to create consistent and visually appealing dashboards that can be accessed and shared across different platforms.

options.text: D. Custom visuals can be formatted and filtered like core visuals
options.explanation: Custom visuals can be formatted and filtered just like core visuals in Power BI. This means that the designer can apply various formatting options, such as colors, fonts, and sizes, and use filters to interact with the data displayed in the custom visual. Develop custom visuals in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: E. Microsoft AppSource is a marketplace for business applications including Power BI visuals
options.explanation: Microsoft AppSource serves as a marketplace for business applications, including Power BI visuals. By exploring Microsoft AppSource, the designer can discover a wide range of custom visuals to enhance their Power BI dashboard and improve the overall user experience. Go through the below links: Microsoft Marketplace | cloud solutions, AI apps, and agents - Search for Charts and you will be amazed by the options that you can use in your dashboard.

explanation: Keep in Mind: 1. What are custom visuals? Custom visuals are additional visual types that extend Power BI’s built-in capabilities. They allow report designers to present data in unique or specialized formats not available in the default Visualizations pane. 2. Where can custom visuals be sourced from? They can be downloaded from Microsoft AppSource, or uploaded manually using PBIVIZ files. 3. What is Microsoft AppSource? AppSource is Microsoft’s marketplace for business applications, including Power BI visuals, Office 365 add-ins, Dynamics 365 extensions, and Azure web apps. 4. What is a PBIVIZ file? A PBIVIZ file is a packaged custom visual file format used to import third-party visuals into Power BI. 5. Are custom visuals supported in Power BI Service? Yes. Custom visuals work seamlessly in both Power BI Desktop and Power BI Service, ensuring consistent functionality across platforms. 6. Can custom visuals be formatted and filtered like core visuals? Yes. Once imported, custom visuals behave like native visuals and support formatting, filtering, and interactivity. 7. Are custom visuals safe to use? Custom visuals from AppSource are vetted by Microsoft. PBIVIZ files from third-party sources should be used cautiously and only if they come from trusted providers. 8. Can custom visuals be shared with others? Yes. When a report containing custom visuals is published or shared, the visuals are included and will render correctly for viewers, assuming they have access to the visual or it's embedded in the report. 9. Do custom visuals require internet access? Some custom visuals, especially those sourced from AppSource, may require internet access to load properly. Offline usage depends on how the visual was built and deployed. 10. Can I build my own custom visuals? Yes. Developers can create custom visuals using the Power BI Visuals SDK and package them as PBIVIZ files for personal use or distribution. Exam Tips: Understand how to import custom visuals using AppSource or PBIVIZ files Know that custom visuals are compatible with both Power BI Desktop and Power BI Service Expect scenario-based multi-answer questions on extending visual capabilities Recognize the difference between core visuals and custom visuals Practice identifying when and how to use custom visuals to meet specific reporting needs Be aware of security and sharing considerations when using third-party visuals Know how to identify visual types using tooltips in the Visualizations pane Understand the role of AppSource as a marketplace for business apps beyond Power BI References: Use report objects - Training | Microsoft Learn Develop custom visuals in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: Match the Element Type with Its Description. Element Types: A. Text box; B. Buttons; C. Shapes; D. Image. Descriptions: 1. Adds rich text like titles with formatting and hyperlinks. 2. Adds interactive controls that perform actions like navigation or drillthrough. 3. Adds decorative or functional visuals like arrows or icons; can include text and actions. 4. Uploads a graphic such as a logo; can also act as a button.

options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Text boxes are used to add rich text like titles with formatting and hyperlinks, making them suitable for adding descriptive text or labels in a report.
This is incorrect option.

A. Text box - Adds rich text like titles with formatting and hyperlinks B. Buttons - Adds interactive controls that perform actions like navigation or drillthrough C. Shapes - Adds decorative or functional visuals like arrows or icons; can include text and actions D. Image - Uploads a graphic such as a logo; can also act as a button Check out the 10 key elements in Power BI under explanation.

explanation: Why Correct A - 1: Text boxes allow you to add formatted text such as titles, instructions, or descriptions. You can apply font styles, colors, alignment, and hyperlinks. B - 2: Buttons are interactive elements that let users perform actions like navigating between pages, triggering bookmarks, or opening URLs. C - 3: Shapes can be decorative or functional. They support styling, text, and can be configured to trigger actions. D - 4: Images can be uploaded to the report page and configured to behave like buttons. Supported formats include BMP, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, and PNG. Keep in Mind: What are elements in Power BI? Elements are visual components that add interest and interactivity to a report. They typically do not use semantic model data. What types of elements are available? Text boxes, buttons, shapes, and images. A. Text box Use to add static or dynamic text (including values from the semantic model) to enhance report storytelling. Supports rich formatting and hyperlinks; dynamic values update with filters when embedded. B. Buttons Enable interactivity by triggering actions like page navigation, drillthrough, or bookmarks. Can be customized with icons, text, and tooltips to guide user behavior. C. Shapes Useful for layout design, emphasis, or grouping visuals; can also trigger actions like buttons. Support text, fill color, borders, and action assignments (e.g., navigation or bookmarks). D. Image Allows insertion of logos or graphics; can also be configured to act as a button with actions. Supports common formats (PNG, JPEG, etc.) and can enhance branding or visual appeal. E. Smart narrative Automatically generates text summaries and insights based on the data in the report. Can be edited and customized; dynamic values update with filters and slicers. F. Q&A Allows users to ask natural language questions and get visual responses based on the data model. Can be pinned as visuals or used to generate dynamic values in text boxes or narratives. G. Visual header tooltip Adds custom tooltips that appear when hovering over a visual’s header. Useful for providing context, instructions, or definitions without cluttering the report. H. Page navigation Prebuilt button type that simplifies linking between report pages. Supports styling and can be used with bookmarks for advanced navigation flows. I. Blank container Used to group multiple visuals or elements for easier alignment and movement. Helps in creating structured layouts and responsive designs. J. Slicer Provides filtering capability directly on the report canvas for user-driven exploration. Supports single or multi-select, dropdowns, sliders, and hierarchical filtering. Can elements perform actions? Yes. Buttons, shapes, and images can be configured to perform actions like navigation, drillthrough, or opening URLs. Do text boxes support hyperlinks? Yes. You can insert hyperlinks and format text with font styles and alignment. Can shapes and images behave like buttons? Yes. Both can be assigned actions and styled to look and function like interactive controls. Are elements part of the Insert ribbon? Yes. All four element types are found in the Elements group under the Insert tab in Power BI. Do elements use semantic model data? Generally no, except when configured to interact with bookmarks or drillthrough actions. Exam Tips: Know the purpose and behavior of each element type Understand which elements support actions and interactivity Expect match-the-pair and scenario-based questions on report layout and design Practice using the Insert ribbon to add and configure elements Recognize how elements enhance user experience without relying on data fields Resources

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is creating a dashboard to display key performance indicators (KPIs) for a marketing team. The KPIs include click-through rate, conversion rate, and cost per acquisition. The designer chooses to present each metric using identical single-value cards aligned in a row. What principle is being applied to improve user comprehension?

options.text: A. Repetition to create consistency and reinforce association
options.explanation: By presenting each metric using identical single-value cards aligned in a row, the designer is applying the principle of repetition. This creates consistency and reinforces the association between the different KPIs, making it easier for users to compare and understand the information.

options.text: B. Contrast to highlight differences between metrics
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Contrast is not the principle being applied in this scenario. While contrast can be used to highlight differences between metrics, in this case, the designer is focusing on consistency and association by using identical single-value cards for each KPI.

options.text: C. Proximity to group related visuals together
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Proximity is not the principle being applied in this scenario. Proximity is used to group related visuals together, but in this case, the designer is aligning the single-value cards in a row to create consistency and reinforce the association between the KPIs.

explanation: Correct Answer Option A - Repetition to create consistency and reinforce association Why Correct Repetition strengthens the layout by using consistent design elements (like identical cards) to tie related objects together. This helps users quickly recognize patterns and interpret similar types of data. Why Others Are Wrong Option B focuses on visual differentiation, not consistency Option C relates to spacing and grouping, not repeated design elements Keep in Mind: 1. What is repetition in report design? Repetition involves using consistent design elements-such as shapes, colors, or layouts-to create visual unity and reinforce relationships. 2. Why is repetition important? It improves readability, speeds up interpretation, and helps users recognize patterns across similar data points. 3. How is repetition applied in dashboards? By using identical visual formats (e.g., single-value cards) for similar metrics or aligning repeated elements in a consistent layout. 4. Can repetition reduce cognitive load? Yes. Familiar visual patterns help users process information faster and reduce the effort needed to interpret data. 5. Is repetition only about visuals? No. It can also apply to text formatting, icons, and layout structures that repeat across sections of a report. Exam Tips: Recognize repetition as a tool for consistency and association Identify repeated design elements like cards, charts, or icons Expect scenario-based questions on layout clarity and user experience Know how repetition improves pattern recognition and reduces cognitive load Practice spotting repetition in sample dashboards and reports References: Design the analytical report layout - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer wants to track performance metrics and visualize progress toward business goals. They are considering using a KPI visual in Power BI. Which of the following are valid use cases for a KPI visual? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. Displaying total sales compared to a target
options.explanation: Using a KPI visual to display total sales compared to a target is a valid use case as it allows the report designer to easily visualize the performance against a specific goal or target.

options.text: B. Showing progress toward a goal over time
options.explanation: Showing progress toward a goal over time is a valid use case for a KPI visual as it helps track the evolution of key metrics and visualize the trend towards achieving business objectives.

options.text: C. Comparing multiple categories side by side
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Comparing multiple categories side by side is not a valid use case for a KPI visual, as KPI visuals are typically used to track and visualize performance against specific targets or goals.

options.text: D. Highlighting variance between actual and target values
options.explanation: Highlighting variance between actual and target values is a valid use case for a KPI visual, as it helps identify areas where performance deviates from the desired target and allows for quick insights into performance gaps.

options.text: E. Tracking employee hires against a monthly goal
options.explanation: Tracking employee hires against a monthly goal is a valid use case for a KPI visual, as it allows the report designer to monitor progress towards a specific target and visualize the effectiveness of recruitment efforts.

explanation: Option A is correct: KPI visuals are commonly used to compare actual values (e.g., total sales) against targets. Option B is correct: KPI visuals show progress toward goals over time using a time series. Option D is correct: KPI visuals highlight variance, which can be favorable or unfavorable, often using colors or icons. Option E is correct: KPI visuals can track any measurable unit (e.g., employee hires) against a goal across time. Option C is incorrect: KPI visuals are not designed for comparing multiple categories side by side. Use bar or column charts for that purpose. Keep in Mind: Key Performance Indicator (KPI) visuals - Power BI | Microsoft Learn 1. What is a KPI visual used for? To communicate performance by comparing actual values to targets and showing progress over time. 2. What are the required components of a KPI visual? A tracked value, a target value, and a time series. 3. Can KPI visuals show variance? Yes. They display the difference between actual and target values, often using color or icons. 4. Are KPI visuals suitable for category comparisons? No. They are best for tracking single metrics over time, not for comparing multiple categories. 5. What types of metrics can be tracked? Sales, hires, loans serviced, students enrolled, any measurable unit with a goal and time series. Exam Tips: Know the three required fields for KPI visuals: value, target, and time Understand how variance is displayed and interpreted Expect questions on choosing visuals based on performance tracking needs Recognize when to use KPI vs. card, gauge, or bar chart Practice configuring KPI visuals with dynamic goals and time-based filters References: Select report visuals - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is building a visual to show sales across multiple product categories. They want to ensure the visual is intuitive and avoids misleading relationships. Which of the following practices are recommended when working with categorical visuals in Power BI? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. Use a bar or column chart to display multiple categories
options.explanation: Using a bar or column chart to display multiple categories is recommended because it allows for easy comparison between different categories. This type of chart is effective in showing the relative size of each category and is intuitive for users to interpret.

options.text: B. Use a line chart with a categorical X-axis to show category relationships
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Using a line chart with a categorical X-axis may not be the best practice when working with categorical visuals in Power BI. Line charts are typically used to show trends over time or continuous data, and may not effectively represent relationships between different categories.

options.text: C. Avoid using too many colors to split data when many category values exist
options.explanation: Avoiding using color to split data when many category values exist is important to prevent confusion and ensure clarity in the visual representation. Using too many colors can make it difficult for users to differentiate between categories and may lead to misleading interpretations of the data.

options.text: D. Sort categorical charts by value to highlight key insights
options.explanation: Sorting categorical charts by value is recommended to highlight key insights and make it easier for users to identify trends or outliers. Sorting the categories in descending or ascending order based on their values can help draw attention to the most important information in the visual.

options.text: E. Use alphabetical sorting to maintain consistency across visuals
options.explanation: Using alphabetical sorting may not always be the best practice when working with categorical visuals, as it may not reflect the natural order or importance of the categories. It is important to sort categories in a way that makes sense for the data being presented and helps in conveying the intended message effectively.

explanation: Option A is correct: Bar and column charts are ideal for displaying data across multiple categories. Option C is correct: When many category values exist, using color to split data (e.g., stacked bar with legend) can make the chart hard to read. Option D is correct: Sorting by value (e.g., descending sales) helps draw attention to the most important data points. Option B is incorrect: Line charts with categorical X-axes imply relationships that may not exist, which can mislead viewers. Option E is incorrect: Alphabetical sorting may not highlight key insights and can reduce the effectiveness of the visual. Keep in Mind: What are categorical visuals? Visuals that display data across discrete categories, such as product names, regions, or departments. Which visuals are best for categorical data? Bar charts and column charts are commonly used for comparing values across categories. Why avoid line charts with categorical X-axes? Lines imply continuity or progression, which can misrepresent relationships between unrelated categories. When should you avoid using color to split data? When there are many category values, color splitting (e.g., stacked bar with legend) can clutter the visual. How should categorical visuals be sorted? Typically by value (ascending or descending), depending on what you want to emphasize. Is alphabetical sorting recommended? Not usually. It may reduce clarity and distract from key insights. References: Select report visuals - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: Match the Visual Type with Its Description. Visual Types: A. Line chart; B. Stacked column chart; C. Area chart; D. Line and stacked column chart; E. Ribbon chart. Descriptions: 1. Ideal for showing trends and values over time. 2. Compares parts of a whole across time periods using stacked bars. 3. Shows cumulative values over time with emphasis on volume. 4. Combines trend lines with category breakdowns in columns. 5. Displays rank changes over time across categories.

options.explanation: This is incorrect match.

The Area chart shows cumulative values over time with an emphasis on volume, matching the description "Shows cumulative values over time with emphasis on volume." The Ribbon chart combines trend lines with category breakdowns in columns, which fits the description "Combines trend lines with category breakdowns in columns."

explanation: Keep in Mind: What are time series visuals? Visuals that display data points across time intervals to show trends, patterns, or changes. Which visuals are best for time series analysis? Line charts, stacked column charts, area charts, line and stacked column charts, and ribbon charts. What does a ribbon chart show? It highlights rank changes over time, useful for comparing categories like regions or products. When should you use a stacked column chart? To show how individual components contribute to a total over time. What’s the benefit of combining line and stacked column charts? It allows simultaneous viewing of trends and category breakdowns. Can area charts be used for time series? Yes. They emphasize volume and cumulative values over time. What you should know about Line Chart? Line charts work well with a consistent flow of data, such as when sales are recorded for every period. If no sales are recorded for some periods, the line chart visual will fill such gaps with a straight line that connects the values of the previous and next periods. If missing values are a possibility, a column chart might be a better visual choice because it helps to avoid the interpretation of a nonexistent trend. Exam Tips: Know which visuals are appropriate for time-based data Understand how each visual communicates trends, comparisons, or rankings Expect match-the-pair and scenario-based questions involving multiple visual types Recognize when to use ribbon charts for rank changes Practice combining visuals to show both trends and breakdowns References: Select report visuals - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer wants to show how product sales are distributed across different stores. They want to use visuals that emphasize proportions rather than actual values. The dataset contains only positive values. Which of the following visuals are appropriate for this scenario? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. 100% Stacked Column chart
options.explanation: A 100% Stacked Column chart is appropriate for showing proportions as it displays the relative contribution of each category to the total. It emphasizes the percentage distribution of sales across different stores.

options.text: B. Pie chart
options.explanation: A Pie chart is suitable for emphasizing proportions as it shows the relationship of parts to a whole. It visually represents the distribution of product sales across different stores in terms of percentages.

options.text: C. Treemap
options.explanation: A Treemap is a good choice for displaying proportions as it visualizes hierarchical data using nested rectangles. It can effectively show the distribution of product sales across different stores based on their relative sizes.

options.text: D. Line chart
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. A Line chart is not ideal for emphasizing proportions as it is more suitable for showing trends over time or comparing values. It focuses on the actual values rather than proportions, making it less appropriate for this scenario.

options.text: E. Doughnut chart
options.explanation: A Doughnut chart is suitable for emphasizing proportions as it is similar to a Pie chart but with a hole in the center. It effectively shows the distribution of product sales across different stores in terms of percentages.

options.text: F. Funnel chart
options.explanation: A Funnel chart is appropriate for showing proportions as it visualizes a process where the values decrease progressively. It can effectively represent the distribution of product sales across different stores in a sequential manner.

explanation: Option A is correct: 100% Stacked Column charts show proportions across categories, with each column totaling 100%. Option B is correct: Pie charts display proportions as slices of a whole. Option C is correct: Treemaps use nested rectangles to show proportions across hierarchical categories. Option E is correct: Doughnut charts are similar to pie charts and show proportions in a circular format. Option F is correct: Funnel charts show proportions across sequential stages, useful for processes like sales pipelines. Option D is incorrect: Line charts are used for trends over time, not for showing proportions of a whole. Keep in Mind: What are proportional visuals? Visuals that show data as part of a whole, emphasizing distribution across categories. When should proportional visuals be used? When you want to show how values are divided across a dimension and all values are either positive or negative. Can proportional visuals handle mixed positive and negative values? No. They should only be used when all values are either positive or all negative. What are examples of proportional visuals? 100% Stacked Column chart, Funnel chart, Treemap, Pie chart, Doughnut chart. Do proportional visuals show actual values? Not always. They often show percentages or relative sizes. Actual values can be revealed using tooltips. What’s the difference between pie and doughnut charts? Both show proportions in a circular format, but doughnut charts have a blank center and can display additional labels. Exam Tips: Know which visuals emphasize proportions vs. actual values Understand that proportional visuals require consistent sign (positive or negative) Expect multi-answer questions comparing visual types and use cases Recognize when to use funnel charts for sequential processes Practice interpreting stacked visuals and treemaps for category distribution References: Select report visuals - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A report designer is creating a Power BI report to display inventory data across multiple stores and product categories. They want to use a visual that allows conditional formatting and supports indicators to highlight specific values. Which Power BI visual should the designer use for this scenario?

options.text: A. Line Chart
options.explanation: The Line Chart visual in Power BI is suitable for showing trends over time or comparing data points. It does not support conditional formatting or indicators to highlight specific values, making it less ideal for the scenario described.

options.text: B. Matrix / Table
options.explanation: The Matrix / Table visual in Power BI is the correct choice for this scenario. It allows the report designer to display data across multiple stores and product categories in a tabular format. It supports conditional formatting and indicators, making it perfect for highlighting specific values. Table Visual Purpose: Displays data in a simple tabular format (rows and columns). Structure: Flat - each column is shown side by side, no hierarchy. Use case: Best for showing detailed records, like transaction lists or inventory items. Features: Supports conditional formatting (colors, icons, data bars). Easy sorting and filtering by column. Good for detailed, rowlevel data. Matrix Visual Purpose: Similar to a pivot table (like in Excel). Structure: Hierarchical - allows grouping and drilling down by rows and columns. Use case: Best for summarizing and comparing data across categories (e.g., sales by region and product). Features: Supports row and column grouping. Can show subtotals and grand totals. Allows drilldown into hierarchies. Conditional formatting also supported.

options.text: C. Card
options.explanation: The Card visual in Power BI is typically used to display a single, high-level metric or KPI. It does not provide the ability to show data across multiple categories or stores, nor does it support conditional formatting and indicators for highlighting specific values.

options.text: D. Clustered column chart
options.explanation: The Clustered Column Chart visual in Power BI is useful for comparing data across different categories or groups. While it can display data for multiple stores and product categories, it does not offer the same level of flexibility for conditional formatting and indicators as the Matrix / Table visual does.

explanation: Keep in Mind: What is a matrix visual? A matrix visual displays data in a grid format, similar to a pivot table, allowing comparisons across multiple dimensions. Can matrix visuals use conditional formatting? Yes. You can apply background colors, font colors, data bars, and icons to highlight values. What are indicators in a matrix? Visual cues like icons or color scales that help users quickly interpret data patterns or thresholds. Can matrix visuals show hierarchical data? Yes. They support drill-downs and expandable row or column groups. A report designer is creating a Power BI report to display inventory data across multiple stores and product categories. They want to use a visual that allows conditional formatting and supports indicators to highlight specific values. Which Power BI visual should the designer use for this scenario? Matrix visuals support grouping, drill-downs, and conditional formatting, while table visuals are simpler and more static. Exam Tips: Know when to use matrix vs. table visuals Understand how to apply conditional formatting and indicators Expect scenario-based questions involving inventory, financials, or performance comparisons Practice configuring matrix visuals with row/column groups and formatting rules Recognize visuals that support hierarchical drill-downs and multi-dimensional layouts

text: A report designer is building a Power BI report to display sales data across cities in the United States. The semantic model includes geospatial information. Which of the following visuals are appropriate for geospatial analysis in Power BI? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. Map visual
options.explanation: The Map visual in Power BI is specifically designed for geospatial analysis and allows the designer to plot data points on a map based on location information. It is ideal for displaying sales data across cities in the United States and highlighting location-based patterns. Overview of Map Visualizations in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn Tips and Tricks for maps (including Bing Maps integration) - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: B. Filled map visual
options.explanation: The Filled map visual in Power BI is another great option for geospatial analysis as it allows the designer to visualize data using shaded areas on a map. This visual can effectively highlight geographical patterns and trends in sales data across different cities. Create and use filled maps (choropleth maps) in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: C. Line chart
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The Line chart visual in Power BI is not suitable for geospatial analysis as it is primarily used to show trends over time or relationships between data points. It does not support the display of geographical information or location-based patterns.

options.text: D. Pie chart
options.explanation: The Pie chart visual in Power BI is not appropriate for geospatial analysis as it is used to show the proportion of different categories within a dataset. It does not provide a geographical representation of data points across cities in the United States.

options.text: E. ArcGIS Maps for Power BI
options.explanation: ArcGIS Maps for Power BI is a specialized mapping tool that integrates with Power BI to provide advanced geospatial analysis capabilities. It offers additional features and customization options for displaying location-based data effectively in Power BI reports. Create an ArcGIS Map in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

explanation:
Option A is correct: The Map visual displays bubbles at geographic coordinates, ideal for dispersed city-level data.

Option B is correct: The Filled map visual shades regions based on values, suitable for broader geographic areas like states or countries.

Option E is correct: ArcGIS Maps for Power BI offers advanced geospatial capabilities, including layers, clustering, and reference maps.

Option C is incorrect: Line charts are used for time series analysis, not for mapping geographic data.

Option D is incorrect: Pie charts show proportions, not spatial distribution.

Keep in Mind:

What are geospatial visuals?

Visuals that display data based on geographic locations such as cities, states, or countries.

What types of map visuals are available in Power BI?

Map visual, Filled map visual, and ArcGIS Maps for Power BI.

When should you use a Map visual?

When data points are dispersed across locations, such as city-level sales.

When is a Filled map more appropriate?

When visualizing data aggregated by region, like state-level totals.

What does ArcGIS Maps offer?

Advanced mapping features like heatmaps, reference layers, and spatial analysis.

Exam Tips: Know the difference between Map and Filled map visuals Understand when to use ArcGIS Maps for advanced geospatial needs Expect scenario-based questions involving location granularity and visual selection Recognize visuals that support formatting options for geographic data Practice using map visuals with latitude/longitude or location fields

text: A report designer is choosing between different visual types to display proportional data. The goal is to select a visual that fits the available space on the report page and makes it easy for users to interpret values. Which of the following are recommended practices when selecting visuals based on layout and readability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A. Use a 100% Stacked Bar chart for wide, short spaces
options.explanation: A 100% Stacked Bar chart is recommended for wide, short spaces as it effectively displays proportional data and utilizes the available space efficiently. This visual type allows users to easily compare the relative proportions of different categories within the data.

options.text: B. Use a 100% Stacked Column chart for narrow, tall spaces
options.explanation: A 100% Stacked Column chart is suitable for narrow, tall spaces as it presents proportional data in a vertical format that fits well in such layouts. This visual type helps users interpret values and compare data across different categories effectively.

options.text: C. Choose visuals based only on data type, not layout
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Choosing visuals based solely on data type and ignoring layout considerations may result in visuals that do not fit well on the report page or make it difficult for users to interpret the data. It is important to consider both data type and layout when selecting visuals.

options.text: D. Prioritize visuals that maximize available space
options.explanation: Prioritizing visuals that maximize available space is essential for ensuring that the report is visually appealing and easy to read. Visuals that effectively use the available space help users quickly understand the data and make informed decisions.

options.text: E. Use visuals that are aesthetically pleasing and readable
options.explanation: Using visuals that are aesthetically pleasing and readable is crucial for enhancing the overall user experience and ensuring that the information is communicated effectively. Visuals that are visually appealing and easy to read encourage user engagement and understanding.

options.text: F. Always use bar charts regardless of layout constraints
options.explanation: Always using bar charts regardless of layout constraints may not be the most effective approach for selecting visuals. It is important to consider the available space on the report page and choose visuals that best fit the layout while also effectively presenting the data.

explanation:
Option A is correct: 100% Stacked Bar charts are easier to read in wide, short spaces due to horizontal bar length.

Option B is correct: 100% Stacked Column charts work better in narrow, tall spaces where vertical height is easier to interpret.

Option D is correct: Choosing visuals that make full use of available space improves clarity and design.

Option E is correct: Aesthetically pleasing visuals enhance user experience and comprehension.

Option C is incorrect: Layout and readability are key factors alongside data type.

Option F is incorrect: Bar charts are not always the best choice; layout and context matter.

Keep in Mind:

Why does layout matter when choosing visuals?

It affects how easily users can interpret data and how well visuals fit the report design.

What’s the difference between bar and column charts?

Bar charts are horizontal; column charts are vertical. Choose based on available space.

Can the same data be shown in different visuals? Y

es. The choice depends on layout, readability, and user experience.

Should visuals be aesthetically pleasing?

Yes. Clean, readable visuals improve engagement and understanding.

Is proportional data best shown in stacked charts?

Often yes, especially 100% stacked charts for comparing relative values.

Exam Tips: Expect scenario-based questions comparing visual choices based on layout Know when to use bar vs. column charts depending on space orientation Understand how visual design affects readability and interpretation Practice choosing visuals that balance data clarity and aesthetic layout Avoid visuals that misrepresent relationships or overcrowd the report page Resources

section: Model data with Power BI
text: A Power BI developer is reviewing the different levels at which filters can be applied in a report. Arrange the following filter levels in order from broadest scope to most specific scope. A. Visual B. Semantic model (Row-level security) C. Page D. Report E. Measure

options.text: B - D - C - A - E
options.explanation: Starting from the broadest scope, the Semantic model (Row-level security) filter applies at the dataset level, affecting all visuals and data in the report. Next, the Report filter applies to the entire report, affecting all pages and visuals within it. Then, the Page filter applies to a specific page in the report, affecting all visuals on that page. The Visual filter applies to a specific visual, allowing for more granular control. Lastly, the Measure filter applies to specific calculations or aggregations within visuals, making it the most specific scope.

options.text: E - D - C - A - B
options.explanation: This is incorrect.

options.text: B - E - D - C - A
options.explanation: This is incorrect.

explanation:
Keep in Mind:

What are the five levels of filtering in Power BI?

Semantic model (Row-level security), Report level, Page level, Visual level, Measure level

What is Row-Level Security (RLS)?

RLS restricts data access at the semantic model level based on user roles. It is enforced before the report loads.

How does report-level filtering work?

Filters applied at the report level affect all pages and visuals within the report.

What is the difference between page-level and visual-level filters?

Page-level filters affect all visuals on a single page. Visual-level filters apply only to the selected visual.

How are filters applied within measures?

Filters are embedded in DAX expressions using functions like CALCULATE, FILTER, or ALL.

Can filters from different levels interact?

Yes. Filters from broader levels can be overridden by more specific ones, depending on context.

Exam Tips: Memorize the filter hierarchy: Semantic model, Report, Page, Visual, Measure Understand that RLS controls data access and is not a visual filter Practice applying filters at each level in Power BI Desktop Expect ordering questions that test your understanding of filter scope Know how DAX filters behave inside calculated measures Be prepared for scenario-based questions that ask which filter level is appropriate for a given task Resources

text: Left Column - Button Actions Back Q&A Bookmark Drillthrough Page navigation Web URL Right Column - Functions A. Navigates to a previously viewed report page B. Opens a natural language query window for data exploration C. Applies a saved report state, including filters and visual visibility D. Navigates to a detailed page based on selected data context E. Directs the user to a specific report page, static or dynamic F. Opens a web link in the default browser, optionally generated by a measure

options.explanation: This option is correct. Back - A. Navigates to a previously viewed report page Q&A - B. Opens a natural language query window for data exploration Bookmark - C. Applies a saved report state, including filters and visual visibility Drillthrough - D. Navigates to a detailed page based on selected data context Page navigation - E. Directs the user to a specific report page, static or dynamic Web URL - F. Opens a web link in the default browser, optionally generated by a measure
This option is incorrect.

explanation: 1. Back - Navigates to a previously viewed report page This button is commonly used in drillthrough scenarios. When users drill into a detail page, the Back button lets them return to the original page they came from. 2. Q&A - Opens a natural language query window for data exploration The Q&A button allows users to type questions in plain language. Power BI interprets the question and returns a visual answer based on the data model. 3. Bookmark - Applies a saved report state, including filters and visual visibility Bookmarks capture the current state of a report page. When activated, they restore that state useful for toggling layouts, resetting filters, or guiding users through a report. 4. Drillthrough - Navigates to a detailed page based on selected data context This button sends users to a drillthrough page that shows more detailed information about a selected item, like a specific customer or product. 5. Page navigation - Directs the user to a specific report page, static or dynamic You can configure this button to take users to a specific page. It can be hardcoded or dynamically determined using a DAX measure that returns a page name. 6. Web URL - Opens a web link in the default browser, optionally generated by a measure This button opens a website. The URL can be static or generated dynamically using a measure that includes filter context, such as a Customer ID in the query string. Refernces: Design reports that behave like apps - Training | Microsoft Learn Learn How Buttons Work in the Power BI Service - Power BI | Microsoft Learn
