text: When uploading a Power BI report (.pbix file) to a workspace, from which sources can you import the file? (Select all that apply)

options.text: OneDrive for work or school
options.explanation: OneDrive for work or school is a valid source to import Power BI report (.pbix) files to a workspace. It allows for seamless integration and access to files stored in OneDrive, enhancing collaboration and sharing capabilities within Power BI.

options.text: Any SharePoint site you have access to
options.explanation: Any SharePoint site that you have access to can be used as a source to import Power BI report (.pbix) files to a workspace. This enables users to leverage the data and resources available in SharePoint for creating and managing Power BI reports.

options.text: Directly from your computer using the Browse option
options.explanation: You can import Power BI report (.pbix) files directly from your computer using the Browse option. This method allows for easy access to local files and simplifies the process of uploading reports to a Power BI workspace.

options.text: From email attachments in Outlook
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Importing Power BI report (.pbix) files from email attachments in Outlook is not a supported source for uploading reports to a workspace. This method may not be secure or efficient for managing and sharing Power BI reports within an organization.

options.text: From a USB drive connected to your computer
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Uploading Power BI report (.pbix) files from a USB drive connected to your computer is not a valid source for importing reports to a workspace. This method may pose security risks and is not recommended for managing and sharing Power BI reports effectively.

explanation: Local computer You can upload a .pbix file directly from your computer using the Import or Browse option in the Power BI Service. OneDrive for work or school If your .pbix file is stored in OneDrive for Business, Power BI can connect to it. Power BI will automatically sync changes approximately every hour, ensuring the workspace report stays updated with the latest version. SharePoint Online (team sites or document libraries) Similar to OneDrive, if the .pbix file is stored in SharePoint Online, Power BI can connect and keep the report in sync. This is especially useful for teams collaborating on shared files. These are the only supported sources for importing .pbix files into a workspace. Other storage options (like local network drives, Dropbox, or Google Drive) are not directly supported for automatic sync. Once imported, the report is hosted in the Power BI Service, and the associated semantic model (dataset) is created in the workspace. References: Publish to Power BI service - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your company stores sensitive financial data in an onpremises SQL Server database. The leadership team wants dashboards in the Power BI Service to refresh automatically every morning with the latest data. However, they insist that: The data must remain onpremises (not moved to the cloud). The connection must be secure. The same setup should also allow automation flows in Power Automate to trigger based on this data. Given this scenario, which of the following is the best solution?

options.text: Export the SQL Server data to Excel daily and upload it manually to Power BI Service.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Exporting SQL Server data to Excel daily and manually uploading it to Power BI Service is not a secure or automated solution. It does not meet the requirement of keeping the data on-premises and securely connecting to Power BI and Power Automate.

options.text: Use a Power BI Gateway to securely connect the onpremises SQL Server to Power BI and other Microsoft cloud services.
options.explanation: Using a Power BI Gateway is the best solution in this scenario as it allows for a secure connection between the on-premises SQL Server and Power BI Service. The data remains on-premises, ensuring compliance with the requirement, and automation flows in Power Automate can also be triggered based on this data.

options.text: Migrate the SQL Server database entirely to Azure SQL Database to enable cloud refresh.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Migrating the SQL Server database entirely to Azure SQL Database is not the best solution as it involves moving the data to the cloud, which contradicts the requirement of keeping the data on-premises. It also does not guarantee a secure connection for the data transfer.

options.text: Schedule a daily email with CSV attachments and import them into Power BI Service.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Scheduling a daily email with CSV attachments and importing them into Power BI Service is not a secure or efficient solution. It does not provide a direct and secure connection between the on-premises SQL Server and Power BI Service, and it does not support automation flows in Power Automate based on the data.

explanation:
How the Onpremises Data Gateway Works

Secure connection: The gateway creates a secure bridge between your onpremises SQL Server and Microsoft cloud services (Power BI, Power Automate, Power Apps, Azure Analysis Services).

Data stays onpremises: The gateway does not move or replicate the database into the cloud. Queries are sent securely through the gateway, and only the results are transmitted.

Scheduled refreshes: You can configure automatic refresh schedules (e.g., every morning) in the Power BI Service. The gateway ensures the latest data is pulled from SQL Server.

Automation flows: The same gateway connection can be used by Power Automate to trigger flows based on SQL Server data, ensuring consistency across services.

Centralized management: IT can manage gateway clusters for high availability and load balancing, ensuring reliability.

Why Others are Wrong:

Uploading PBIX manually - Would not refresh automatically and causes versioning issues.

Moving SQL Server data to the cloud - Violates the requirement that sensitive financial data must remain onpremises.

Direct connection without gateway - Not secure and not supported for scheduled refreshes or automation.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your organization is evaluating how to connect onpremises data sources to Power BI. They want to understand the differences between Standard mode and Personal mode gateways. Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Standard mode allows multiple users to connect to multiple onpremises data sources, making it suitable for complex enterprise scenarios.
options.explanation: Standard mode gateway is designed to allow multiple users to connect to multiple onpremises data sources, making it ideal for complex enterprise scenarios where different users need access to various data sources for reporting and analysis within Power BI.

options.text: Personal mode can only be used with Power BI and cannot be shared with other users.
options.explanation: Personal mode gateway is restricted to use with Power BI only and cannot be shared with other users. It is intended for individual users who need to connect their Power BI reports to onpremises data sources without sharing the gateway with others.

options.text: Personal mode requires installation on a local computer that must remain online for the gateway to function.
options.explanation: Personal mode gateway requires installation on a local computer that must remain online for the gateway to function. This means that the computer hosting the personal gateway must be continuously connected to the internet to ensure data connectivity for Power BI reports.

options.text: Standard mode is limited to a single user and cannot connect to multiple data sources.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Standard mode gateway is not limited to a single user; instead, it allows multiple users to connect to multiple data sources. This flexibility makes it suitable for scenarios where multiple users across an organization need to access different onpremises data sources.

options.text: Personal mode supports Power BI, Power Automate, and Power Apps equally.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Personal mode gateway is specifically designed for use with Power BI and does not support other Microsoft cloud services like Power Automate and Power Apps. It is tailored for Power BI users who need to connect to onpremises data sources within their reports.

options.text: Standard mode can be managed centrally and supports multiple Microsoft cloud services beyond Power BI.
options.explanation: Standard mode gateway can be centrally managed, allowing administrators to control access and configurations across multiple users and data sources. Additionally, it supports various Microsoft cloud services beyond Power BI, enabling integration with other cloud-based applications and services for comprehensive data connectivity.

explanation: Two types of on-premises gateways are: Standard mode - Allows multiple users to connect to multiple on-premises data sources and is suitable for complex scenarios. Personal mode - Allows one user to connect to data sources. This type of gateway can only be used with Power BI. It can't be shared with other users, making it suitable for situations where you're the sole report creator in your organization. You'll install the gateway on your local computer, which needs to stay online for the gateway to work. Use a Power BI gateway to connect to on-premises data sources - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: When you work in the cloud and interact with an element connected to an onpremises data source, which of the following actions occur? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The cloud service creates a query and encrypted credentials, then sends them to the gateway queue.
options.explanation: When working in the cloud and interacting with an on-premises data source, the cloud service creates a query and encrypts credentials before sending them to the gateway queue for further processing.

options.text: The gateway cloud service analyzes the query and pushes the request to Microsoft Azure Service Bus.
options.explanation: The gateway cloud service receives the query and request from the cloud service, analyzes it, and then pushes the request to Microsoft Azure Service Bus for routing and communication with the on-premises data source.

options.text: Service Bus sends the pending requests to the gateway.
options.explanation: Microsoft Azure Service Bus plays a crucial role in the communication process by sending the pending requests from the cloud service to the gateway for further processing and connection to the on-premises data source.

options.text: The gateway decrypts the credentials and connects to one or more onpremises data sources.
options.explanation: Upon receiving the query and credentials from the cloud service, the gateway decrypts the credentials and establishes a secure connection to one or more on-premises data sources to retrieve the required data.

options.text: The gateway sends the query to the data source to be executed.
options.explanation: The gateway, after establishing a secure connection with the on-premises data source, sends the query to the data source to be executed and fetch the requested data for further processing.

options.text: The results are returned from the data source to the gateway, then back to the cloud service for use.
options.explanation: Once the data source executes the query and processes the request, the results are returned to the gateway. The gateway then forwards the results back to the cloud service for utilization and analysis in the cloud environment.

explanation: When you're working in the cloud and interacting with an element that is connected to an on-premises data source, the following actions occur: The cloud service creates a query and the encrypted credentials for the on-premises data source. The query and credentials are sent to the gateway queue for processing. The gateway cloud service analyzes the query and pushes the request to Microsoft Azure Service Bus. Service Bus sends the pending requests to the gateway. The gateway gets the query, decrypts the credentials, and then connects to one or more data sources with those credentials. The gateway sends the query to the data source to be run. The results are sent from the data source back to the gateway and then to the cloud service. The service then uses the results. Use a Power BI gateway to connect to on-premises data sources - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are a Power BI analyst. One of your reports is connected to a SharePoint Online document library. Recently, the report fails to refresh in the Power BI Service, and the error message indicates that the connection could not be established. What is the first action you should take to troubleshoot this issue?

options.text: Reinstall Power BI Desktop on your computer.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reinstalling Power BI Desktop on your computer is not the first action you should take to troubleshoot a connection issue with SharePoint Online. This action is unlikely to resolve the issue related to data source credentials.

options.text: Ensure that your data source credentials for SharePoint in the Power BI Service are up to date.
options.explanation: Ensuring that your data source credentials for SharePoint in the Power BI Service are up to date is the correct first action to take when troubleshooting a connection issue. Outdated or incorrect credentials can prevent the report from refreshing successfully.

options.text: Install and configure an onpremises data gateway for SharePoint Online.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Installing and configuring an on-premises data gateway for SharePoint Online is not the immediate action to take in this scenario. The issue is likely related to data source credentials, and setting up a data gateway may not address the root cause of the connection problem.

options.text: Delete the dataset and reimport the SharePoint file from scratch.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and re-importing the SharePoint file from scratch should be considered as a last resort after verifying and updating the data source credentials. This action may result in data loss and should only be done if other troubleshooting steps have failed.

explanation: Cloud services, such as SharePoint, do not require a gateway because the data is already in the cloud. You only need to provide your authorization credentials to set up a data source connection. If your report fails to refresh, ensure that your data source credentials are up to date. Use a Power BI gateway to connect to on-premises data sources - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are a Power BI analyst preparing a report for the HR team. The report uses employee data stored in SharePoint Online. The HR manager insists that the report must always show the latest employee data without requiring manual updates. What should you do to resolve this situation?

options.text: Reimport the employee dataset into Power BI Desktop every time new data is available.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Re-importing the employee dataset into Power BI Desktop every time new data is available is not a scalable solution and would require manual intervention, which goes against the HR manager's requirement for automatic updates to always show the latest data.

options.text: Configure a scheduled refresh in the Power BI Service to automatically update the dataset at defined times.
options.explanation: Configuring a scheduled refresh in the Power BI Service is the correct solution to automatically update the dataset at defined times. This ensures that the report always shows the latest employee data without requiring manual updates, meeting the HR manager's requirement.

options.text: Install an onpremises data gateway for SharePoint Online.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Installing an on-premises data gateway for SharePoint Online is not necessary in this situation as the data is already stored in SharePoint Online. This solution is more relevant when connecting to on-premises data sources, not cloud-based sources like SharePoint Online.

options.text: Delete the dataset and upload the latest version manually whenever needed.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and uploading the latest version manually whenever needed is not an efficient solution as it would require manual intervention and does not meet the HR manager's requirement for automatic updates to always show the latest data.

explanation: Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn Steps to Configure Scheduled Refresh: Go to the Power BI Service Navigate to the workspace where you published the HR report. Locate the dataset Under the workspace’s Datasets + dataflows section, find the dataset linked to your report. Open settings Click the More options (…) next to the dataset - select Settings. Expand Scheduled refresh In the dataset settings, expand the Scheduled refresh section. Enable refresh Toggle Keep data up to date to On. Set refresh frequency Define the refresh schedule (e.g., Daily at 8:00 AM) so the HR team always sees the latest employee data. You can set multiple times per day if needed. Authentication check Since the data source is SharePoint Online, ensure the correct credentials are entered under Data source credentials. Use OAuth2 authentication for SharePoint Online. Save settings Save the refresh schedule. Power BI will now automatically update the dataset at the defined times. So, configure a scheduled refresh in the Power BI Service for the dataset, ensuring credentials are set correctly and defining a daily refresh time so the HR team always sees the latest data.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You want to set up a scheduled refresh for a semantic model in Power BI. The steps below are out of order. Arrange them in the correct sequence: Select the Refresh frequency and ensure the correct time zone is selected. Hover over the semantic model and select the Schedule refresh icon. Add the time(s) you want the refresh to occur. Go to the workspace where the report and semantic model are located. On the Settings page, turn on the Scheduled refresh feature. When finished configuring, select Apply.

options.explanation: The correct sequence for setting up a scheduled refresh for a semantic model in Power BI is to first go to the workspace where the report and semantic model are located (Step 4), then hover over the semantic model and select the Schedule refresh icon (Step 2). After that, turn on the Scheduled refresh feature on the Settings page (Step 5), select the Refresh frequency and ensure the correct time zone is selected (Step 1), add the time(s) you want the refresh to occur (Step 3), and finally, when finished configuring, select Apply (Step 6).

This sequence is incorrect because it starts with selecting the Refresh frequency and ensuring the correct time zone is selected (Step 1), which should actually be done after turning on the Scheduled refresh feature (Step 5). The correct sequence should begin with going to the workspace where the report and semantic model are located (Step 4), followed by hovering over the semantic model and selecting the Schedule refresh icon (Step 2), turning on the Scheduled refresh feature on the Settings page (Step 5), adding the time(s) you want the refresh to occur (Step 3), and finally, when finished configuring, selecting Apply (Step 6).

explanation: Set up a refresh schedule: Before you can set up a refresh schedule, you need to have created a gateway connection. To set up a refresh schedule for your semantic model, follow these steps: Go to the workspace where the report and semantic model are located. Hover over the semantic model for which you want to set up the schedule and then select the Schedule refresh icon. On the Settings page, turn on the Scheduled refresh feature. Select the Refresh frequency and ensure that the correct time zone is selected. Add the time(s) that you want the refresh to occur. You can configure up to eight daily time slots, if your semantic model is on shared capacity, or 48 time slots on Power BI Premium. When you have finished configuring the scheduled refresh, select Apply. Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Which of the following statements about scheduled refresh in Power BI is correct?

options.text: Scheduled refresh always occurs exactly at the time you set.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect. Scheduled refresh in Power BI does not always occur exactly at the time set by the user. There can be delays in the initiation of the refresh process.

options.text: Power BI initiates scheduled refreshes on a besteffort basis, aiming to start within 15 minutes of the scheduled time, but delays of up to one hour can occur.
options.explanation: This statement is correct. Power BI initiates scheduled refreshes on a best-effort basis, aiming to start within 15 minutes of the scheduled time. However, delays of up to one hour can occur due to various factors such as system load, network issues, or dataset complexity.

options.text: Scheduled refresh can only be run manually by the dataset owner.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect. Scheduled refresh in Power BI can be automated and set up to run at specific intervals without manual intervention by the dataset owner. This automation helps ensure data is up-to-date without requiring manual intervention.

options.text: Scheduled refresh is guaranteed to complete within five minutes of the scheduled time.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect. Scheduled refresh in Power BI does not guarantee completion within five minutes of the scheduled time. The duration of the refresh process can vary depending on the size of the dataset, complexity of the data transformations, and other factors impacting data refresh.

explanation: Lines from Learning Path: While you can set a time for the refresh, be aware that the refresh might not take place at that exact time. Power BI starts scheduled refreshes on a best effort basis. The goal is to initiate the refresh within 15 minutes of the scheduled time slot, but a delay of up to one hour can occur if the service can't allocate the required resources sooner. References: Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Put the following steps in the correct order to successfully promote a semantic model in Power BI: Options (scrambled): A. Go to the workspace in Power BI Service. B. Select the Endorsement setting and choose Promote/Certified C. Ensure you have write permissions on the workspace. D. Open the settings page for the semantic model.

options.text: B - Go to the workspace in Power BI Service A - Ensure you have write permissions D - Select the Endorsement setting and choose Promote/Certified C - Open the settings page for the semantic model
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Ensuring you have write permissions on the workspace is crucial before attempting to promote a semantic model in Power BI. Without the necessary permissions, you will not be able to make any changes or endorsements to the model.

options.text: C - Ensure you have write permissions on the workspace. A - Go to the workspace in Power BI Service. D - Open the settings page for the semantic model. B - Select the Endorsement setting and choose Promote/Certified
options.explanation: The correct order to successfully promote a semantic model in Power BI is to first ensure you have write permissions on the workspace, then go to the workspace in Power BI Service, open the settings page for the semantic model, and finally select the Endorsement setting and choose Promote/Certified. This sequence of steps ensures a smooth and successful promotion process.

explanation: Manage and promote semantic models - Training | Microsoft Learn Here’s the correct order of steps to successfully promote a semantic model in Power BI: C. Ensure you have write permissions on the workspace. (You need sufficient rights to change endorsement settings.) A. Go to the workspace in Power BI Service. (Navigate to the workspace where the semantic model is located.) D. Open the settings page for the semantic model. (Access the dataset/semantic model settings.) B. Select the Endorsement setting and choose Promote/Certified. (Apply the endorsement to mark the semantic model as promoted or certified.) Exam Tips: Expect scenario questions like: “Which permission level is required to promote a semantic model?” - Write permissions (Contributor/Member/Admin). “Where do you apply endorsement?” - In the semantic model settings in Power BI Service. “What’s the difference between Promote and Certified?” - Promote = userdriven, Certified = organizationapproved.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your company has deployed several reports in Power BI Premium capacity. The Sales Performance report is opened daily by hundreds of users, but the underlying semantic model is refreshed only once a week. Executives complain about slow load times when opening the report. To improve the experience, you enable query caching. Which of the following advantages will query caching provide in this scenario?

options.text: Improves performance of reports, dashboards, and dashboard tiles.
options.explanation: Query caching will improve the performance of reports, dashboards, and dashboard tiles by storing the results of previous queries. This means that when users access the Sales Performance report, the data will be retrieved from the cache instead of running the query again, resulting in faster load times.

options.text: Respects bookmarks and default filters.
options.explanation: Query caching respects bookmarks and default filters set in the report. This ensures that users will see the data based on their selected filters and bookmarks, even when the query results are cached.

options.text: Cached query results are specific to each user.
options.explanation: Cached query results are specific to each user, meaning that each user will see the data based on their individual interactions with the report. This personalized caching improves the user experience and ensures data accuracy.

options.text: All security labels are followed.
options.explanation: Query caching ensures that all security labels and permissions are followed when retrieving cached query results. This means that sensitive data will only be accessible to users who have the appropriate permissions, maintaining data security.

options.text: Reduces the load on your dedicated capacity.
options.explanation: By enabling query caching, you can reduce the load on your dedicated capacity in Power BI Premium. Since the query results are cached and reused, there is less strain on the capacity to process and retrieve data, leading to improved performance for all users.

options.text: Queries are cached for every single interaction with the report.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Queries are not cached for every single interaction with the report. Instead, query caching stores the results of previous queries to improve performance. This means that users will benefit from faster load times without the need to rerun the same queries repeatedly.

explanation: Query Caching is a feature that maintains cache results on a user and report basis. Query caching reduces load time and increases query speed, especially for semantic models that aren't refreshed often and are accessed frequently. This service is only available to users with Microsoft Fabric, Power BI Premium or Power BI Embedded. The caching is performed the first time a user opens the report. The service only does query caching for the initial page that they land on. In other words, queries aren't cached when you interact with the report. In simple words, Imagine you have a big Excel file with thousands of rows. Every time you open it, Excel has to recalculate everything from scratch - which takes time. Now, think of Power BI reports built on large datasets. When lots of people open the same report, Power BI normally has to run the same queries again and again to fetch the data. That slows things down. Query caching is like Power BI saying: “Hey, I already did this calculation once. Let me save the result in a quickaccess memory spot.” Next time someone opens the same report, Power BI just shows the saved result instead of rerunning the whole query. Several benefits to using query caching include: Improvement of the performance of reports, dashboards, and dashboard tiles. It respects bookmarks and default filters. Cached query results are specific to the user. All security labels are followed. It reduces the load on your dedicated capacity. Youtube Video: Troubleshooting DAX performance? Clear the Power BI model cache! References: Boost performance with query caching (Fabric or Premium capacity) - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are preparing a Power BI report for a leadership meeting. The dataset is scheduled to refresh every morning at 8 AM, but you notice that new data has just been added to the source and the meeting starts in 30 minutes. Waiting for the next scheduled refresh isn’t an option, and you also want to quickly test whether your gateway and data source configuration are working correctly. What should you do?

options.text: Reconfigure the scheduled refresh to run immediately.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reconfiguring the scheduled refresh to run immediately may not be the quickest solution as it might take some time to update the settings and initiate the refresh. This option may not be suitable for the urgent situation where you need to test the gateway and data source configuration quickly.

options.text: Delete the dataset and reimport the latest data manually.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and re-importing the latest data manually is a time-consuming process, especially when you are short on time before the meeting starts. This option is not efficient for quickly testing the gateway and data source configuration.

options.text: Install a new gateway before refreshing.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Installing a new gateway before refreshing is unnecessary and time-consuming in this scenario. It is not directly related to quickly testing the gateway and data source configuration for the upcoming meeting.

options.text: Perform an ondemand refresh by selecting the Refresh now icon on the semantic model.
options.explanation: Performing an on-demand refresh by selecting the Refresh now icon on the semantic model is the most suitable option in this situation. It allows you to quickly test whether your gateway and data source configuration are working correctly without waiting for the next scheduled refresh. This option provides immediate results and is the most efficient choice for the urgent need to update the data before the meeting.

explanation: Perform an on-demand refresh In addition to the scheduled refreshes, you can refresh a semantic model at any time by performing an on-demand refresh. This type of refresh doesn't affect the next scheduled refresh time. For example, you might want to refresh now because you need to view the most recent data and can't wait for the next refresh time, or you might want to test your gateway and data source configuration. To perform an on-demand refresh, hover over the semantic model that you want to refresh and then select the Refresh now icon. Exam Tips: OnDemand Refresh in Power BI Where to do it: In the Power BI service, go to the workspace and locate the dataset (semantic model). Action: Select the Refresh now icon next to the dataset. Effec​t: Power BI immediately connects to the data source and reloads the dataset with the latest data. Scope: This refresh applies to the dataset only; all reports and dashboards built on that dataset will reflect the updated data once the refresh completes. Difference from Scheduled Refresh: Ondemand refresh = manual, triggered by a user. Scheduled refresh = automatic, based on a defined schedule. Keep in Mind: Power BI Desktop Refresh - Updates the dataset and all report visuals in your local file. Service Refresh (Refresh now) - Updates the dataset stored in the Power BI service, which then updates reports and dashboards built on that dataset. References: Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are responsible for maintaining several Power BI reports in your organization. One of the managers asks when the employee dataset was last refreshed and whether any errors have occurred. You also want to confirm when the next refresh is scheduled. What is the quickest way to check this information?

options.text: Open Power BI Desktop and reload the dataset manually.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Opening Power BI Desktop and manually reloading the dataset is not the quickest way to check the last refresh time, any errors, or the next scheduled refresh. This method involves unnecessary manual intervention and does not provide a comprehensive overview of the refresh status and history.

options.text: View the list of semantic models in the workspace to check refresh status and history.
options.explanation: Viewing the list of semantic models in the workspace is the quickest way to check the refresh status, history, and schedule of the employee dataset. This option allows you to easily access the necessary information without the need for manual intervention or reconfiguration of connections.

options.text: Reconfigure the gateway connection to force a refresh.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reconfiguring the gateway connection to force a refresh is not the quickest way to check the last refresh time, errors, or the next scheduled refresh. This method involves unnecessary steps and may disrupt the existing configuration without providing a direct overview of the dataset's refresh status.

options.text: Delete the dataset and reimport it to see the latest refresh time.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and re-importing it to see the latest refresh time is not the quickest way to check the refresh status, history, or schedule. This method is time-consuming, disruptive, and may result in data loss or inconsistencies. It is not recommended for quickly checking the dataset refresh information.

explanation: You can check the refresh status and history at any time. This feature is useful if you want to find out when the last refresh occurred and when the next one is scheduled. It is also good practice to check the status of your semantic models occasionally to check if refresh errors have occurred. A quick way to check the refresh status is to view the list of semantic models in a workspace. Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Choosing the Right Endorsement Scenario 1: A product semantic model is ready for others to use and should be highlighted for reuse. Scenario 2: A sales semantic model must be authoritative, governed, and restricted to avoid confusion. Options: A. Promotion B. Certification

options.text: Scenario 1 - A Scenario 2 - A
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Promotion is suitable for the scenario where a product semantic model is ready for others to use and should be highlighted for reuse. It helps increase visibility and encourages adoption of the model by making it more accessible to users.

options.text: Scenario 1 - B Scenario 2 - B
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Certification is the appropriate choice for the scenario where a sales semantic model must be authoritative, governed, and restricted to avoid confusion. Certification ensures that the model meets specific standards, is reliable, and is controlled to prevent unauthorized changes or misuse.

options.text: Scenario 1 - A Scenario 2 - B
options.explanation: Promotion (Choice A) is the correct option for Scenario 1 as it aims to highlight the model for reuse. Certification (Choice B) is the correct option for Scenario 2 as it ensures the model is authoritative, governed, and restricted to prevent confusion.

explanation: Power BI provides three ways to endorse your semantic models: Promotion - Enables you to highlight content that you think is valuable, worthwhile, and ready for others to use. It encourages the collaborative spread of content within the organization. Certification - Request certification for a promoted semantic model. Certification can be a highly selective process, so only the truly reliable and authoritative semantic models are used across the organization. Master data - Being labeled as master data means that the data item is regarded by the organization as being core, single-source-of-truth data, such as customer lists or product codes. This is a feature from Microsoft Fabric. Exam Tips: Promotion - Highlight valuable content, encourage collaboration, but not formally validated Certification - Strict governance, authoritative models Master Data - Core, singlesourceoftruth items Keep in Mind: Power BI currently supports endorsement for: Semantic models Dataflows Reports Apps References: Manage and promote semantic models - Training | Microsoft Learn Promote and Certify Power BI Content with Endorsement - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are monitoring a semantic model in Power BI Service. While checking the workspace, you notice a small warning icon next to one of the semantic models. What should you do to find out more about the issue?

options.text: Ignore the warning icon and wait for the next scheduled refresh.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Ignoring the warning icon and waiting for the next scheduled refresh may not be the best approach as the issue could potentially impact the functionality of the semantic model. It is important to investigate the warning to ensure the model is functioning correctly.

options.text: Select the warning icon to view the refresh error message and details.
options.explanation: Selecting the warning icon to view the refresh error message and details is the correct action to take in this situation. This will provide you with more information about the issue that is causing the warning icon to appear, allowing you to address and resolve the issue effectively.

options.text: Delete the semantic model and reupload it.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the semantic model and re-uploading it is a drastic measure and may not be necessary to resolve the issue indicated by the warning icon. It is recommended to first investigate the error message and details provided by selecting the warning icon before considering deleting and re-uploading the model.

options.text: Reinstall Power BI Desktop to fix the issue.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reinstalling Power BI Desktop is not a solution to fix the issue with the semantic model in Power BI Service. The warning icon is specific to the semantic model in the workspace, and reinstalling the desktop application will not address the underlying issue causing the warning. It is important to focus on investigating the specific issue related to the semantic model.

explanation: Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn If a semantic model displays a small warning icon, you'll know that the semantic model is currently experiencing an issue. Select the warning icon to get more information. You should also check the refresh history occasionally to review the success or failure status of past synchronization cycles. Exam Tips: Report - A collection of pages with visuals (charts, tables, maps). - Think of it like a detailed magazine where each page tells a different part of the story. Dashboard - A single page that shows tiles (pinned visuals) from one or more reports. - Think of it like a car dashboard - a quick snapshot of the most important info at once. App - A packaged version of reports and dashboards from a workspace, shared with end users. - Think of it like a mobile app - clean, easy to use, and read-only for consumers. Workspace - The backstage area where teams build, edit, and manage reports, datasets, and dashboards. - It’s the collaboration hub before content is published as an app. Semantic Model (formerly Dataset) - The data model that powers reports - includes tables, relationships, measures, and calculations. - Think of it like the engine under the hood that makes visuals run. Dataflow - A reusable pipeline to clean and transform data before loading into reports. - Think of it like a water filter that prepares clean data for everyone to use. Paginated Report - A report designed for printing or exporting, with precise formatting (like invoices or statements). - Think of it like a PDF report - pixel-perfect and page-ready. KPI (Key Performance Indicator) - A visual that shows progress toward a goal (e.g., sales vs target). - Think of it like a speedometer showing if you’re on track. Dataset vs Data Source - Data source = where the raw data lives (Excel, SQL, etc.). - Dataset/semantic model = the structured version inside Power BI used for reporting.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are responsible for monitoring several critical Power BI reports. One of the finance managers complains that yesterday’s refresh didn’t update the dataset correctly, and they suspect a refresh error occurred. You need to confirm when the last refresh happened, whether it succeeded, and when the next refresh is scheduled. What is the most appropriate action to take?

options.text: Reinstall Power BI Desktop and reload the dataset manually.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reinstalling Power BI Desktop and reloading the dataset manually will not provide information about the last refresh, its success, or the next scheduled refresh. This action is unnecessary and does not address the issue at hand.

options.text: Open the semantic model’s Settings page and select Refresh history to view detailed logs.
options.explanation: Opening the semantic model's Settings page and selecting Refresh history is the most appropriate action as it allows you to view detailed logs of the last refresh, including information on its success or failure. This will help you confirm what happened during the previous refresh and when the next refresh is scheduled.

options.text: Delete the dataset and reimport it to check the refresh status.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and re-importing it is a drastic and unnecessary step to check the refresh status. It may result in data loss and does not provide a direct solution to the issue of confirming the last refresh, its success, and the next scheduled refresh.

options.text: Configure a new scheduled refresh to overwrite the existing one.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Configuring a new scheduled refresh to overwrite the existing one is not the best course of action as it does not address the immediate need to confirm the status of the last refresh and when the next refresh is scheduled. It may also disrupt the current data flow and cause unnecessary complications.

explanation: To view the refresh history, open the semantic model's settings page and then select Refresh history. Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are managing several Power BI reports for your organization. One of your datasets suddenly stops refreshing, and you discover that the refresh schedule has been disabled by the service. Which of the following situations could have caused this?

options.text: No user visited the report or any dashboard built on the semantic model for two months.
options.explanation: If no user visits the report or any dashboard built on the semantic model for a certain period, the service may disable the refresh schedule to optimize resources as there seems to be no active usage of the dataset.

options.text: The refresh failed four consecutive times.
options.explanation: When a dataset refresh fails multiple times consecutively, the service may disable the refresh schedule to prevent further failures and potential issues with the data integrity.

options.text: The service detected invalid or expired credentials requiring a configuration update.
options.explanation: If the service detects invalid or expired credentials for the dataset, it may disable the refresh schedule until the credentials are updated to ensure secure and accurate data refreshes.

options.text: You manually changed the consecutive failures threshold to a lower value.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Manually changing the consecutive failures threshold to a lower value would not directly cause the refresh schedule to be disabled. The service typically disables the schedule based on actual refresh failures or lack of usage, not on the threshold configuration.

explanation: Lines from Learning Path: If no user visits the report or any dashboard built on the semantic model, Power BI disables the refresh schedule after two months of inactivity. The refresh schedule is also disabled after four consecutive failures or when the service detects an unrecoverable error that requires a configuration update, such as invalid or expired credentials. It is not possible to change the consecutive failures threshold. Keep in Mind: Inactivity Rule If no user visits a report or dashboard built on a semantic model for two months, Power BI automatically disables the refresh schedule. This prevents unnecessary resource usage for unused content. Failure Rule The refresh schedule is disabled after four consecutive refresh failures. Failures can occur due to issues like connectivity, invalid queries, or service interruptions. The threshold of four failures is fixed. It cannot be changed. Unrecoverable Error Rule If Power BI detects an unrecoverable error requiring configuration updates (e.g., invalid or expired credentials), the refresh schedule is disabled. Admins or dataset owners must fix the configuration before reenabling refresh. Reenable Refresh After refresh is disabled (due to inactivity, failures, or errors), you must manually reenable the schedule once the issue is resolved. References: Configure a semantic model scheduled refresh - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You are managing a large Power BI semantic model that contains five years of sales data. Refreshing the entire dataset takes several hours and often fails due to resource limits. Your manager asks you to ensure that the dataset refreshes quickly and reliably, but without reloading all historical data every time. What should you do?

options.text: Delete all historical data and keep only the last 10 days of sales data in the dataset.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting historical data may lead to loss of valuable insights and trends from past sales data. Keeping only the last 10 days of sales data may not be sufficient for comprehensive analysis and reporting.

options.text: Manually refresh the dataset every day in Power BI Desktop to avoid scheduled refresh issues.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Manually refreshing the dataset every day in Power BI Desktop is not a scalable solution for large datasets with historical data. It is time-consuming and prone to human error, and does not address the issue of long refresh times and failures.

options.text: Increase the scheduled refresh frequency to run every hour so the dataset stays current.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Increasing the scheduled refresh frequency to run every hour may overload the system and cause performance issues, especially with large datasets. It may not solve the problem of long refresh times and failures due to resource limits.

options.text: Configure incremental refresh in Power BI Desktop by defining a refresh policy, then publish to Power BI Service.
options.explanation: Configuring incremental refresh in Power BI Desktop allows you to define a refresh policy that only updates new or modified data since the last refresh. This approach helps in quickly refreshing the dataset without reloading all historical data every time, ensuring efficient and reliable refreshes.

explanation: Option 1 - Configure incremental refresh in Power BI Desktop. This ensures only recent data (e.g., last 10 days) is refreshed, while historical data remains untouched, resulting in quicker, more reliable refreshes and reduced resource consumption. The Incremental refresh feature in Power BI is a popular feature because it allows you to refresh large semantic models quickly and as often as you need, without having to reload historical data each time. Traditionally, complex code was required for running incremental refreshes, but you can now define a refresh policy within Power BI Desktop. Quicker refreshes - Only data that needs to be changed gets refreshed. For example, if you have five years' worth of data, and you only need to refresh the last 10 days because that is the only data that has changed, the incremental refresh will refresh only those 10 days of data. Undoubtedly, the time it takes to refresh 10 days of data is much shorter than five years of data. Exam Tips: With incremental refresh and real-time data: Fewer refresh cycles for fast-changing data are needed: DirectQuery mode gets the latest data updates as queries are processed, without requiring a high refresh cadence. Refreshes are faster: Only the most recent data that changed needs to be refreshed. Refreshes are more reliable: Long-running connections to volatile data sources aren't necessary. Queries to source data run faster, reducing potential for network problems to interfere. Resource consumption is reduced: Less data to refresh reduces overall consumption of memory and other resources in both Power BI and data source systems. Large semantic models are enabled: Semantic models with potentially billions of rows can grow without the need to fully refresh the entire model with each refresh operation. Setup is easy: Incremental refresh policies are defined in Power BI Desktop with just a few tasks. When Power BI Desktop publishes the report, the service automatically applies those policies with each refresh. Configure incremental refresh settings - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You want to configure an incremental refresh policy in Power BI to optimize performance for a large dataset. The process involves several steps, but they are listed below out of order. Publish changes to Power BI Service. Define the filter parameters. Use the parameters to apply a filter. Define the incremental refresh policy. Delete the dataset and reupload it. Reinstall Power BI Desktop.

options.explanation: This is incorrect option. This sequence starts with defining the incremental refresh policy, followed by defining the filter parameters, applying the filter using the parameters, and finally publishing the changes to the Power BI Service. However, deleting the dataset and re-uploading it should not be part of the process as it is not necessary for configuring an incremental refresh policy.

The correct sequence begins with defining the filter parameters to specify the data to be refreshed incrementally. Next, the parameters are used to apply a filter to the dataset, followed by defining the incremental refresh policy to optimize performance. Finally, the changes are published to the Power BI Service to implement the incremental refresh strategy. Keep in Mind: Bookmark this link when you need to do incremental refresh. Configure incremental refresh for Power BI semantic models - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

This is incorrect option. This sequence starts with defining the filter parameters, then moves to deleting the dataset and re-uploading it, followed by applying the filter using the parameters, defining the incremental refresh policy, and finally publishing the changes to the Power BI Service. However, deleting and re-uploading the dataset is not a standard step in configuring an incremental refresh policy.

explanation: You can define an incremental refresh policy to solve this business problem. This process involves the following steps: Define the filter parameters. Use the parameters to apply a filter. Define the incremental refresh policy. Publish changes to Power BI service. Youtube Video: How to use INCREMENTAL REFRESH for Datasets (PRO) and Dataflows (PREMIUM) in Power BI Configuring Incremental Refresh in Power BI References: Configure incremental refresh settings - Training | Microsoft Learn Configure incremental refresh for Power BI semantic models - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

text: You are working with a very large sales dataset in Power BI Desktop that spans 10 years. Because the PBIX file is limited by your computer’s memory, you configure incremental refresh by defining two date/time parameters: RangeStart and RangeEnd. After publishing the report to the Power BI Service, your manager asks how these parameters actually work in practice.

options.text: In Power BI Desktop, RangeStart and RangeEnd act as a filtering window, restricting the data loaded during development.
options.explanation: In Power BI Desktop, RangeStart and RangeEnd are used to define the incremental refresh window, allowing only data within that range to be loaded during development. This helps manage the dataset size and optimize performance during report creation.

options.text: RangeStart and RangeEnd are only used in Desktop and have no role once published to the Service.
options.explanation: RangeStart and RangeEnd parameters are not limited to Power BI Desktop; they are essential for incremental refresh in the Power BI Service as well. These parameters define the range of data to refresh in the dataset, ensuring that only the necessary data is loaded for efficient processing.

options.text: Defining RangeStart and RangeEnd automatically deletes all historical data outside the chosen range.
options.explanation: Defining RangeStart and RangeEnd does not automatically delete historical data outside the chosen range. Instead, it helps in loading and refreshing only the incremental data within the specified range, reducing the dataset size and improving performance without affecting the existing historical data.

explanation: Define filter parameters Whether you are using incremental refresh or not, large semantic models are commonly filtered when they are imported into Power BI Desktop because the PBIX file is limited by the memory resources that are available on the desktop computer. For incremental refresh, the semantic models are filtered by two date/time parameters: RangeStart and RangeEnd. These parameters have a dual purpose. In Power BI Desktop, they are the filtering window because they restrict the used data to the range that is listed in the start and end dates. After they have been published to the service, the parameters are taken over to be the sliding window to determine what data to pull in. References: Configure incremental refresh settings - Training | Microsoft Learn Configure incremental refresh for Power BI semantic models - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: You have defined two parameters, RangeStart and RangeEnd, in Power BI Desktop to configure incremental refresh. To correctly apply the filter on your dataset’s OrderDate column, which condition should you use in the Filter Rows window?

options.text: Keep rows where OrderDate ≥ RangeStart and OrderDate < RangeEnd.
options.explanation: The correct condition for applying the filter on the dataset's OrderDate column in the Filter Rows window is to keep rows where OrderDate is greater than or equal to RangeStart and less than RangeEnd. This condition ensures that only the rows within the specified date range are included in the dataset for incremental refresh. Configure incremental refresh for Power BI semantic models - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: Keep rows where OrderDate ≤ RangeStart and OrderDate > RangeEnd.
options.explanation: This condition is incorrect as it specifies to keep rows where OrderDate is less than or equal to RangeStart and greater than RangeEnd. This condition would not filter the dataset correctly based on the defined parameters for incremental refresh.

options.text: Keep rows where CustomerName ≥ RangeStart and CustomerName < RangeEnd.
options.explanation: This condition is incorrect as it specifies to keep rows where CustomerName is greater than or equal to RangeStart and less than RangeEnd. Since the parameters defined for incremental refresh are related to OrderDate, using CustomerName in the filter condition would not apply the correct filter to the dataset.

options.text: Keep rows where OrderDate = RangeStart OR OrderDate = RangeEnd.
options.explanation: This condition is incorrect as it specifies to keep rows where OrderDate is equal to either RangeStart or RangeEnd. This condition would not capture the range of dates specified by the parameters for incremental refresh, leading to incorrect filtering of the dataset.

explanation: Correct Answer: Option 1 - Apply the filter on the OrderDate column with the condition: OrderDate is after or equal to RangeStart OrderDate is before RangeEnd Incorrect but plausible: Option 2 - Wrong direction of comparison; excludes intended range. Option 3 - Wrong column; parameters must be applied to a date column, not text. Option 4 - Equality only would miss all rows between RangeStart and RangeEnd. References: Configure incremental refresh settings - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: When defining an incremental refresh policy in Power BI, which of the following fields/settings must you configure?

options.text: Turn on the Incremental refresh option in the Incremental refresh window.
options.explanation: Turning on the Incremental refresh option is essential to enable the incremental refresh policy in Power BI. This setting allows Power BI to incrementally refresh the dataset based on the defined criteria.

options.text: Define the period of historical data to store (e.g., last 5 years + current year).
options.explanation: Defining the period of historical data to store is crucial for the incremental refresh policy. This setting determines how far back in time the data will be stored and considered for incremental refresh.

options.text: Define the period of data to incrementally refresh (e.g., last 10 days).
options.explanation: Defining the period of data to incrementally refresh specifies the timeframe for which new data will be loaded incrementally during each refresh. This setting helps in efficiently updating the dataset with recent data.

options.text: Configure the removal of data older than the defined historical period (e.g., remove years older than 5 years).
options.explanation: Configuring the removal of data older than the defined historical period is necessary to manage the dataset's size and ensure that only relevant data is retained. This step helps in maintaining the dataset's performance and storage efficiency.

options.text: Reinstall Power BI Desktop before every refresh.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Reinstalling Power BI Desktop before every refresh is not a required step for configuring an incremental refresh policy. It is unrelated to defining the incremental refresh settings and would not impact the incremental refresh process.

options.text: Delete the dataset and reupload it to trigger refresh.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting the dataset and re-uploading it to trigger a refresh is not a recommended approach for implementing an incremental refresh policy. Incremental refresh is designed to update the dataset with new data efficiently, without the need for manual intervention like deleting and re-uploading the dataset.

explanation: Define the incremental refresh policy When you have filtered the data, you can define the incremental refresh policy for the data table, which sets up the refresh process. Right-click the applicable table and then select Incremental refresh. On the Incremental refresh window that displays, turn on the Incremental refresh option. Then, configure the refresh as required. In this example, you will define a refresh policy to store data for five full calendar years, plus data for the current year up to the current date, and incrementally refresh 10 days of data. The first refresh operation in Power BI service will load the historical data for the last five years. The subsequent refresh operations are incremental, and they will refresh the data that was changed in the last 10 days up to the current date. The incremental refreshes will also remove calendar years that are older than five years prior to the current date. References: Configure incremental refresh settings - Training | Microsoft Learn Configure incremental refresh and real-time data for Power BI semantic models - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your organization shares semantic models across multiple workspaces. A developer plans to change a semantic model used by several teams. Before making the change, they want to understand how it will affect downstream reports and dashboards. Which of the following are advantages of performing impact analysis in this scenario?

options.text: Identifies downstream reports and dashboards that depend on the semantic model.
options.explanation: Performing semantic model impact analysis helps identify downstream reports and dashboards that rely on the semantic model being changed. This allows the developer to understand the potential impact of their changes on other teams and ensure that critical reports are not disrupted. Semantic model impact analysis - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: Helps avoid breaking reports in other workspaces when changes are made.
options.explanation: By conducting semantic model impact analysis, developers can avoid breaking reports in other workspaces when making changes to the semantic model. This ensures that all teams continue to have access to accurate and up-to-date data without any disruptions.

options.text: Provides visibility into crossworkspace dependencies.
options.explanation: Semantic model impact analysis provides visibility into cross-workspace dependencies, allowing developers to see how changes to the semantic model may affect reports and dashboards in different workspaces. This insight is crucial for maintaining data consistency and integrity across the organization.

options.text: Automatically updates all dependent reports when the semantic model changes.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Semantic model impact analysis does not automatically update all dependent reports when the semantic model changes. It helps identify the reports that need to be updated manually to reflect the changes in the semantic model, ensuring that all reports remain accurate and relevant.

options.text: Allows you to assess risk before implementing changes.
options.explanation: One of the advantages of performing semantic model impact analysis is that it allows developers to assess the risk before implementing changes. This helps in making informed decisions about the modifications to the semantic model and ensures that any potential risks are mitigated before they impact the organization's data analytics processes.

explanation: Perform semantic model impact analysis: When you make changes to a semantic model, or are considering making changes, it's important to be able to assess the potential impact of those changes on downstream reports and dashboards that depend on that semantic model. Performing this impact analysis is useful for semantic models that are shared across workspaces, where it's complicated to get a clear picture of downstream dependencies. To perform semantic model impact analysis, select the impact analysis button on the semantic model card. The following screenshot demonstrates there's an additional report that depends on the semantic model. The report is in a different workspace, and the semantic model is shared with that workspace. References: Data source impact analysis - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your organization has multiple workspaces with dozens of semantic models. Different teams are building reports, but executives complain that numbers don’t match across dashboards because teams are using different versions of the same data. You’ve been asked to ensure consistency and promote a healthy data culture. What is the best action to take?

options.text: Endorse the most uptodate and highestquality semantic models as the single source of truth, so report creators reuse them.
options.explanation: Endorsing the most up-to-date and highest-quality semantic models as the single source of truth ensures consistency across reports and promotes a healthy data culture. By having a centralized source of truth, report creators can reuse these models, leading to accurate and aligned data across dashboards.

options.text: Allow every team to create and publish their own semantic models without restrictions, encouraging flexibility.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Allowing every team to create and publish their own semantic models without restrictions may lead to inconsistencies and discrepancies in the data. This approach does not promote a healthy data culture and can result in confusion among executives when numbers do not match across reports.

options.text: Restrict reuse of semantic models across workspaces to prevent confusion, but avoid endorsing any models.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Restricting the reuse of semantic models across workspaces without endorsing any models can create silos and hinder collaboration. Without a centralized source of truth, teams may continue to use different versions of the data, leading to discrepancies in reports and confusion among executives.

options.text: Delete older semantic models from all workspaces and force teams to rebuild reports from scratch.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Deleting older semantic models from all workspaces and forcing teams to rebuild reports from scratch is a drastic and inefficient solution. It can disrupt ongoing work, waste time and resources, and may not address the underlying issue of data inconsistency. It is not the best action to promote a healthy data culture and ensure consistency in reports.

explanation: Endorsement in Power BI can be Promoted (recommended for reuse) or Certified (formally validated by data governance teams). Together, these ensure that report creators know which semantic models are reliable and should be reused. Single Source of Truth for Finance Reports Endorse the official financial semantic model so all teams use the same revenue, expense, and profit definitions. Standardized Sales Metrics Across Regions Endorse a global sales semantic model to ensure regional teams report sales consistently without redefining KPIs. Exam Tips: Endorsement applies to datasets, reports, dashboards, and apps. Promoted content is userdriven; anyone can promote what they think is useful. Certified content is organizationdriven; only authorized people can certify. Endorsed content is easier to discover because it appears higher in search and is labeled. Certification is often tied to governance policies and ensures compliance. Endorsement helps reduce duplication by guiding users to trusted sources. Promoted content encourages collaboration and sharing across teams. Certified content provides official, authoritative datasets for consistent reporting. Endorsement is visible in both Power BI service and Excel when connecting to Power BI data. Exam scenarios often ask: “Which endorsement type ensures official organizational approval?” - Certification. In short: Promotion = “This looks good, please use it.” Certification = “This is officially approved, you can trust it.” References: Manage and promote semantic models - Training | Microsoft Learn Promote and Certify Power BI Content with Endorsement - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

explanation: Power BI provides three ways to endorse your semantic models: Promotion - Enables you to highlight content that you think is valuable, worthwhile, and ready for others to use. It encourages the collaborative spread of content within the organization. Certification - Request certification for a promoted semantic model. Certification can be a highly selective process, so only the truly reliable and authoritative semantic models are used across the organization. Master data - Being labeled as master data means that the data item is regarded by the organization as being core, single-source-of-truth data, such as customer lists or product codes. section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your organization uses Power BI Premium capacity. The Finance dashboard is opened daily by hundreds of users, but the underlying semantic model is refreshed only once a month. Executives complain about slow load times when opening the dashboard. You decide to enable query caching for the semantic model. Question: Which of the following advantages will query caching provide in this scenario?

options.text: Faster load times for reports, dashboards, and tiles.
options.explanation: Enabling query caching for the semantic model will result in faster load times for reports, dashboards, and tiles as the cached results can be quickly retrieved without the need to reprocess the data each time the dashboard is opened.

options.text: Respects bookmarks and default filters.
options.explanation: Query caching respects bookmarks and default filters set by users, ensuring that the cached results are tailored to each user's specific view and preferences when accessing the Finance dashboard.

options.text: Cached query results are specific to each user.
options.explanation: Cached query results are specific to each user, meaning that the data retrieved from the cache will be personalized based on the user's interactions and selections within the dashboard, providing a more customized experience.

options.text: All security labels are followed.
options.explanation: With query caching enabled, all security labels and permissions are followed, ensuring that users only see the data they are authorized to access, maintaining data security and compliance within the Finance dashboard.

options.text: Reduces load on Premium capacity.
options.explanation: Query caching reduces the load on Premium capacity by storing and retrieving pre-processed query results, reducing the need for repeated data processing and optimizing resource utilization within the Power BI environment.

options.text: Queries cached for every single interaction with the report.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Queries are not cached for every single interaction with the report. Instead, query caching stores and retrieves pre-processed results based on user interactions, reducing the processing time and improving performance for subsequent accesses to the Finance dashboard.

explanation: To access and configure query caching, follow these steps: Go to a semantic model in your workspace and open its Settings page. In this example, you enable query caching for SalesModel. Select the semantic models tab and expand the Query Caching options, as shown in the following image. On the Query Caching page, choose one of the available options. The default option is that query caching is turned off; however, you can also select Off, which turns off query caching for the specific semantic model in question. If you select On, query caching is turned on for this specific semantic model only. For this example, you'll select On for your semantic model because you want to apply query caching to your specific semantic model. Exam Tips: Keep in mind about Query Caching: Definitio​n: Query caching saves the results of queries in Power BI Premium or Embedded capacity, reducing load times. Scope: It applies only to Import semantic models. Not Supported: Query caching does not work with DirectQuery or LiveConnect connections (like Azure Analysis Services or SQL Server Analysis Services). Availability: Only available in Premium capacity or Power BI Embedded workspaces. First Load Behavio​r: The cache is created the first time a user opens a report page. Initial Page Only: Caching is performed for the initial landing page of the report, not all pages. Performance Benefit: It avoids recalculating queries from the semantic model, improving report responsiveness. Consistency: Ensures more predictable performance by offloading query processing to cloud resources. User Basis: Cache results are maintained per user and per report. Refresh Impact: When the dataset is refreshed, cached results are invalidated and rebuilt. Governance: Admins can enable or disable query caching at the dataset level. Capacity Consideration: Query caching uses Premium capacity resources, so enabling it should be balanced with other workloads. Limitations: It doesn’t accelerate queries for complex DirectQuery models. Exam Focus: Know when query caching applies (Import models, Premium capacity) and when it doesn’t (DirectQuery, nonPremium). Scenario Example: If a workspace is in Premium capacity and uses Import mode, enabling query caching speeds up report load times. User Experience: End users see faster loading dashboards and reports after the first query is cached. Security: Cached results respect rowlevel security (RLS) rules. Embedded Use: Improves performance for apps embedding Power BI reports via Power BI Embedded. Best Practice: Use query caching for frequently accessed Import datasets in Premium capacity. Exam Tip: Expect questions like “Does query caching work with DirectQuery?” - Answer: No. References: Boost performance with query caching (Fabric or Premium capacity) - Training | Microsoft Learn Query caching in Power BI Premium - Power BI | Microsoft Learn
