text: A dashboard in Power BI is showing outdated numbers, and the report creator suspects the issue comes from the underlying model or data source. Which advantage does the lineage view provide in this situation?

options.text: Shows the relationships between all artifacts in a workspace.
options.explanation: The lineage view in Power BI Service shows the relationships between all artifacts in a workspace, including reports, datasets, dataflows, and data sources. This can help the report creator identify any dependencies or connections that may be causing the outdated numbers in the dashboard.

options.text: Displays the data sources from which semantic models get their data.
options.explanation: By displaying the data sources from which semantic models get their data, the lineage view can help the report creator trace back to the original source of the data. This can be crucial in identifying any issues or discrepancies in the data that may be affecting the dashboard.

options.text: Provides gateway information if the data source is connected via an onpremises gateway.
options.explanation: The lineage view in Power BI Service provides gateway information if the data source is connected via an on-premises gateway. This can help the report creator understand the data flow and connectivity between the data source, semantic model, and the dashboard, potentially pinpointing any issues related to data refresh or connectivity.

options.text: Shows the last refresh time of semantic models.
options.explanation: The lineage view shows the last refresh time of semantic models, allowing the report creator to see when the data was last updated. This information can be valuable in determining if the outdated numbers in the dashboard are due to a lack of recent data refresh.

options.text: Indicates whether a semantic model is certified or promoted.
options.explanation: The lineage view indicates whether a semantic model is certified or promoted, providing additional context on the reliability and quality of the data being used in the dashboard. This can help the report creator assess the trustworthiness of the data and make informed decisions on data usage.

options.text: Automatically fixes refresh issues without user intervention.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The lineage view does not automatically fix refresh issues without user intervention. It provides visibility into the data flow and relationships between artifacts but does not perform any automated fixes. The report creator would still need to investigate and address any refresh issues manually.

explanation: Understanding the flow of data from the data source to its destination can be a challenge. Questions like "What happens if I move this data?" or "Why isn't this report up to date?" can be hard to answer. They might require a team of experts or deep investigation to understand. Power BI's data lineage view helps you answer these questions. In lineage view, you see the lineage relationships between all the artifacts in a workspace. 1. How to access Lineage view? 2. How lineage view looks like? Every workspace automatically has a lineage view. You need at least a Contributor role in the workspace to view it. In this view, you see all the workspace artifacts and how the data flows from one artifact to another. You see the data sources from which the semantic models get their data. If a data source is connected via an on-premises gateway, the gateway information is added to the data source card. On semantic models, you see the last refresh time, and if the semantic model is certified or promoted. Youtube Video: Looking at the Lineage View in Power BI (October 2019) Exam Tips: Expect questions like below however in the format of scenario based: What does Lineage View show in a workspace? - The relationships between datasets, reports, dashboards, and dataflows. Can Lineage View display external data sources? - Yes, it shows connections to external sources feeding datasets. How does Lineage View help analysts? - It helps trace data origin and understand dependencies. If a dataset is deleted, what does Lineage View indicate? - It shows broken links to reports or dashboards depending on that dataset. Can you refresh datasets directly from Lineage View? - Yes, refresh actions can be triggered from Lineage View. Does Lineage View show sensitivity labels? - Yes, sensitivity labels applied to datasets or reports are visible in Lineage View. How does Lineage View assist with troubleshooting? - It highlights missing or broken connections between artifacts. Can Lineage View show dataflows feeding multiple datasets? - Yes, it visually maps dataflows to all connected datasets. Is Lineage View available in Power BI Desktop? - No, it is only available in the Power BI service. How does Lineage View support governance? - It provides transparency into data sources, transformations, and usage across the workspace. References: Use lineage and impact analysis - Training | Microsoft Learn Data lineage - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

text: The Sales team wants the dataset to refresh automatically every morning at 7 AM so that executives always see uptodate numbers in their dashboards. Where should you configure the scheduled refresh for this semantic model?

options.text: A. Power BI Service
options.explanation: The scheduled refresh for datasets in the Power BI Service can be configured to automatically refresh data at specific intervals. This is the correct choice because the dataset has already been published to the Power BI Service, and this is where the scheduled refresh functionality is available. Configure scheduled refresh - Power BI | Microsoft Learn Keep in Mind: The maximum number of scheduled refreshes per day depends on the license/capacity: Power BI Pro: Up to 8 scheduled refreshes per day. Power BI Premium per user (PPU) and Premium / Fabric capacity (F SKU / EM / P / Fabric capacity): Up to 48 scheduled refreshes per day.

options.text: B. Power BI Desktop
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Power BI Desktop is used for creating and designing reports and models, but it does not have the capability to schedule automatic refreshes for datasets. The scheduled refresh functionality is only available in the Power BI Service where the dataset is published.

options.text: C. AppSource
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. AppSource is a marketplace for finding and installing applications that work with Power BI, but it is not the correct location to configure scheduled refresh for datasets. The scheduled refresh feature is specific to the Power BI Service where the dataset is hosted.

explanation: Correct Answer: A. Power BI Service - Scheduled refreshes are configured in the Power BI Service after publishing the semantic model. Power BI Service - Workspace - Semantic model (dataset) - Settings - Scheduled refresh Why: Power BI Desktop is used to build the semantic model. Once published, all refresh configuration (credentials, gateways, schedule) is managed in the Power BI Service. Scheduled refresh only runs from the Service. Incorrect: B. Power BI Desktop - Refresh can be done manually here, but scheduled refresh cannot be configured. C. AppSource - This is a marketplace for apps and visuals, not for configuring refresh schedules. Keep in Mind for Exam: Typical steps Go to Power BI Service Open the workspace containing the Sales semantic model Select the semantic model (dataset) Open Settings Configure Scheduled refresh (set to daily at 7:00 AM) Ensure credentials and gateway (if on-premises) are configured References: Data refresh in Power BI - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Which of the following statements about workspace roles in Power BI are wrong?

options.text: Workspace roles allow you to selectively exclude specific reports or dashboards from being shared.
options.explanation: Workspace roles in Power BI do not allow you to selectively exclude specific reports or dashboards from being shared. The roles determine the level of access and permissions a user has within the workspace, but they do not offer the ability to exclude specific content.

options.text: RowLevel Security (RLS) is enforced for all roles (Viewer, Contributor, Member, Admin).
options.explanation: Row-Level Security (RLS) is not enforced for all roles in Power BI workspaces. RLS is a feature that allows you to restrict data access based on user roles or other criteria, but it is not automatically enforced for all roles like Viewer, Contributor, Member, and Admin.

options.text: Contributors can manage workspace settings and assign roles to others.
options.explanation: Contributors in Power BI workspaces do not have the ability to manage workspace settings and assign roles to others. This level of control is typically reserved for higher roles like Members and Admins who have more administrative privileges.

options.text: Members can publish apps from the workspace.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Members in Power BI workspaces do have the ability to publish apps from the workspace. This feature allows them to package and distribute content to a broader audience outside of the workspace.

options.text: Admins have full control, including managing permissions and deleting the workspace.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Admins in Power BI workspaces do have full control, including managing permissions and deleting the workspace. They have the highest level of administrative privileges and can oversee all aspects of the workspace.

options.text: Workspace roles can be assigned to individuals, security groups, Microsoft 365 groups, and distribution lists.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Workspace roles in Power BI can indeed be assigned to individuals, security groups, Microsoft 365 groups, and distribution lists. This flexibility allows for efficient management of access and permissions within the workspace.

explanation: Viewer Most restrictive role. Can only view and interact with reports, dashboards, and semantic models. Cannot create, edit, or delete content. RowLevel Security (RLS) is enforced for this role. Ideal for stakeholders who consume data but don’t modify it. Contributor Can create, edit, and delete content (reports, dashboards, semantic models). Cannot manage workspace settings or assign roles. Suitable for team members actively developing and maintaining Power BI content. Member Has all Contributor permissions. Can manage workspace settings and assign roles to others. Can publish apps from the workspace. Best for team leads or power users who need more control. Admin Full control over the workspace. Can manage permissions, assign roles, delete the workspace, and oversee all actions. Keep in Mind: Expect scenario questions like: Which role can publish an app? - Member/Admin Do workspace edits automatically update the app? - No, republish required Can app users edit reports? - No, viewonly Which role can add new datasets to a workspace? - Contributor/Member/Admin Who can delete reports in a workspace? - Contributor/Member/Admin. Contributors can delete content they created; Members/Admins can delete any content. Which role can only view dashboards and reports without editing? - Viewer Who can assign roles to other users in a workspace? - Admin Which role can update app content after publishing? - Member/Admin Can Contributors publish apps? - No Which role has full control over workspace settings? - Admin Who can share datasets with others outside the workspace? - Member/Admin Which role can create dashboards but not publish them as apps? - Contributor Can Viewers see datasets in the workspace? - Yes, but readonly. Viewers can see datasets, but: They cannot build new reports unless explicitly granted Build permission They generally can’t explore datasets directly Which role can remove users from a workspace? - Admin Who can edit reports created by others in the workspace? - Contributor/Member/Admin. Requires appropriate permissions (and the report not being in a read-only state). Which role is best for executives who only need to consume reports? - Viewer Can Members change workspace permissions? - No, only Admins Which role can refresh datasets in the workspace? - Contributor/Member/Admin. Contributors can refresh datasets they own or have permission for. Who can configure rowlevel security (RLS) in datasets? - Contributor/Member/Admin. Typically limited to dataset owners or users with edit permissions. Which role can manage workspace capacity and premium settings? - Admin References: Understand sharing models - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: A business analyst has created a Power BI report and wants to share it with a few specific colleagues within the organization. The requirement is that only selected users should be able to view the report, and access should be controlled securely. What is the best way to share the Power BI report in this scenario?

options.text: A. Publish the report as a Power BI App for the entire organization
options.explanation: Publishing the report as a Power BI App for the entire organization would not meet the requirement of restricting access to only selected users. This option would make the report available to all users within the organization, rather than securely sharing it with specific colleagues.

options.text: B. Share the report directly with specific users using Power BI Service sharing options
options.explanation: Sharing the report directly with specific users using Power BI Service sharing options is the best way to securely control access to the report. This option allows the business analyst to choose exactly who can view the report, ensuring that only the selected colleagues have access to the information.

options.text: C. Export the report to PDF and send it via email
options.explanation: Exporting the report to PDF and sending it via email does not provide a secure way to control access to the report. Once the PDF is sent, the business analyst would have no control over who can view the report, and it could potentially be shared with unintended recipients.

options.text: D. Store the report in Power BI Desktop and share the file (.pbix)
options.explanation: Storing the report in Power BI Desktop and sharing the file (.pbix) is not a secure way to control access to the report. Sharing the file directly would allow anyone with access to the file to view its contents, rather than restricting access to only selected users as required in the scenario.

explanation:
Power BI Service allows users to share reports directly with specific individuals or groups. This ensures:

Controlled access (only selected users can view)

Secure sharing within the organization

Retention of interactivity (unlike PDF or Excel export)

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your organization has multiple teams creating reports in different workspaces. The Executive team wants a curated collection of dashboards and reports packaged together and distributed to the entire company. They also want to ensure that updates can be tested in a staging area before being published, so employees only see finalized versions. Which of the following advantages of Power BI Apps apply in this scenario?

options.text: Allows packaging multiple dashboards and reports into a single cohesive app experience.
options.explanation: Power BI Apps allow the Executive team to package multiple dashboards and reports into a single cohesive app experience, making it easier to distribute curated collections of content to the entire company.

options.text: Eliminates the need to manage permissions for individual items.
options.explanation: By using Power BI Apps, the Executive team can eliminate the need to manage permissions for individual items, simplifying the process of granting access to the curated dashboards and reports.

options.text: Provides flexibility to distribute apps via direct link, Apps marketplace, AppSource, or automatic installation.
options.explanation: Power BI Apps provide flexibility in distributing apps via direct links, Apps marketplace, AppSource, or automatic installation, allowing the Executive team to choose the most suitable distribution method for the entire company.

options.text: Enables updates to be tested in the workspace before republishing the finalized app.
options.explanation: With Power BI Apps, updates can be tested in the workspace before republishing the finalized app, ensuring that employees only see the approved and finalized versions of the curated dashboards and reports.

options.text: Each workspace can publish multiple apps simultaneously.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Each workspace can only publish one app, not multiple.

options.text: Content included in the app must originate from the same workspace.
options.explanation: Power BI Apps require that all content included in the app must originate from the same workspace, ensuring that the curated collection of dashboards and reports are cohesive and consistent in their source.

explanation: Power BI Apps - Streamlined Sharing Purpose Share collections of dashboards, reports, and content with a larger audience. Avoids the need for workspace membership or itembyitem sharing. Useful for distributing curated content to groups or the entire organization. Key Advantages Package multiple items into a single cohesive app experience. Simplifies permissions by eliminating itemlevel management. Flexible access: via direct link, Apps marketplace, AppSource, or automatic installation by admin. Controlled updates: workspace acts as a staging area; republish only finalized versions. Consistency: ensures users always see the latest approved content. Limitations Each workspace can publish only one app. Content included in the app must originate from the same workspace. Tight coupling between app and workspace simplifies management but restricts crossworkspace packaging. Keep in Mind: Definition: A Power BI app is a packaged collection of dashboards and reports. Purpose: Apps simplify distribution of content to large groups of users. Single Package: An app can contain multiple dashboards and reports from one workspace. Publishing: Only Members and Admins of a workspace can publish apps. Audience: Apps are shared with users or groups in your organization. Access Control: You decide who can access the app when publishing. Updates: Changes in the workspace don’t automatically update the app; you must republish. Navigation: Apps provide a custom navigation pane for end users. ReadOnly: Users consuming apps cannot edit content; they only view. Distribution: Apps can be distributed via direct link or through the Power BI service “Apps” section. Permissions: App permissions are separate from workspace roles. Customization: Publishers can customize app branding (logo, colors, descriptions). Multiple Audiences: Apps can be published with different audiences, each seeing tailored content. Mobile Friendly: Apps are accessible on Power BI mobile apps. Security: Rowlevel security (RLS) applies when users view content in apps. Licensing: Users need appropriate Power BI licenses (Pro or Premium per user/capacity) to access apps. Versioning: Republishing an app overwrites the previous version for all users. Discoverability: Apps appear in the “Apps” section of Power BI service for easy access. Best Practice: Use apps to distribute finalized, production-ready content, not drafts. Exam Focus: Know the difference between workspace roles vs. app permissions, and how publishing works. References: Understand sharing models - Training | Microsoft Learn

text: Evaluate the following statements about creating and updating a Power BI App. Mark each as True or False.

options.text: When creating an app, you must provide a name, description, and optional theme color. - True You can add content from multiple workspaces into a single app. - False Publishing the app generates a shareable link for distribution. - True To update an app, you open the workspace and select the Edit app (pencil icon). - True Changes made to the app are immediately visible to all users without republishing. - False Republishing the app ensures users automatically see the updated version. - True
options.explanation: This is correct option.

options.text: When creating an app, you must provide a name, description, and optional theme color. - True You can add content from multiple workspaces into a single app. - True Publishing the app generates a shareable link for distribution. - True To update an app, you open the workspace and select the Edit app (pencil icon). - True Changes made to the app are immediately visible to all users without republishing. - True Republishing the app ensures users automatically see the updated version. - True
options.explanation: This is incorrect option.

explanation: To create, update, or unpublish a Power BI app, follow these steps: (How to Publish, View, & Edit App in Power BI?) Create a Power BI App Set up the app: In the workspace, select Create app. Provide a name, description, and optional theme color. Add a support site link and contact information if needed. Add content: On the Content tab, select Add content to include dashboards, reports, or other items from the workspace. Arrange the content in the desired order. Publish the app: Once the setup and content are finalized, click Publish app. A shareable link will be generated for distribution. Update a Power BI App Open the workspace: Navigate to the workspace associated with the app. Select the Edit app pencil icon. Make changes: Modify the app's content, setup, or other settings as needed. Changes remain in the workspace until republished. Republish the app: Select Update app to apply the changes. Users with access will automatically see the updated version. Unpublish a Power BI App Unpublish the app: In the workspace, select More options (...) > Unpublish app. Youtube Video: Create your first Power BI APP in 5 minutes! text: Your company has published a Power BI App that includes dashboards for Sales, Marketing, and Finance. The leadership team wants each department to only see the dashboards relevant to their work, while still managing everything from a single app. They also want to avoid creating multiple apps or duplicating workspaces. Which of the following describes the correct use of Audiences in this scenario?

options.text: Create separate audiences for Sales, Marketing, and Finance, each with access to their relevant dashboards.
options.explanation: Creating separate audiences for Sales, Marketing, and Finance allows you to control access to specific dashboards based on department roles, ensuring that each team only sees the relevant data within the Power BI App.

options.text: Audiences allow you to tailor content visibility so users only see data relevant to their roles.
options.explanation: Audiences in Power BI enable you to customize content visibility, ensuring that users only have access to the data and dashboards that are pertinent to their roles within the organization.

options.text: Audiences require creating multiple apps for each department.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Audiences do not require the creation of multiple apps for each department. Instead, they provide a way to manage content visibility within a single Power BI App, avoiding the need for duplication of workspaces.

options.text: Audiences simplify content management by controlling visibility at the audience level within one app.
options.explanation: Audiences simplify content management by allowing you to control visibility at the audience level within one app. This means that you can manage access to different dashboards for various departments without creating separate apps.

options.text: Audiences automatically grant edit permissions to each department’s dashboards.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Audiences do not automatically grant edit permissions to each department's dashboards. Instead, they focus on controlling visibility and access to specific content based on the audience settings defined within the Power BI environment.

options.text: Audiences enhance security by ensuring sensitive data is only visible to authorized groups.
options.explanation: Audiences enhance security by ensuring that sensitive data is only visible to authorized groups, such as specific departments. This helps to maintain data privacy and confidentiality within the Power BI environment.

explanation: Audiences Audiences in Power BI apps allow you to tailor the content visibility and access for different groups of users within your organization. This feature is particularly useful when you need to distribute specific dashboards, reports, or other content to distinct teams or departments while maintaining centralized control over permissions and visibility. What is an Audience in Power BI Apps? An audience in Power BI apps is a defined group of users who have access to a specific subset of content within an app. By creating multiple audiences, you can customize which content is visible to each group, ensuring that users only see the data relevant to their roles or responsibilities. For example, you might create separate audiences for sales, marketing, and finance teams, each with access to different reports and dashboards. Example, Imagine you build one Power BI app for your company: Sales Team Audience - They only see sales dashboards. Finance Team Audience - They only see finance reports. Executives Audience - They see highlevel summary dashboards. Same app, but different content for each group. Audiences = tailored content groups inside one Power BI app. Why Use Audiences? Using audiences simplifies content management and enhances security. Instead of creating multiple apps or workspaces for different teams, you can manage all content within a single app and control visibility at the audience level. Saves time: You don’t need to publish separate apps for each department. Keeps things clean: People only see what’s relevant to them. Improves security: Sensitive data is shown only to the right audience. References: Create a Power BI app - Training | Microsoft Learn

text: Your company has published a Power BI App for the Finance team. The app is hosted in a workspace that is not in Premium capacity. Later, the IT department moves the workspace into a Premium capacity (F64 or higher Fabric capacity) so that more employees can access the content. Which of the following statements about licensing are correct in this scenario?

options.text: To create or update the app, you need a Power BI Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) license.
options.explanation: Having a Power BI Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) license is necessary to create or update the app in a workspace that has been transitioned to Premium capacity. This licensing requirement ensures that only authorized users with appropriate access can make changes to the app.

options.text: If the workspace is not in Premium capacity, all users need Pro or PPU licenses to view the app.
options.explanation: In a workspace that is not in Premium capacity, all users must possess Power BI Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) licenses to be able to view the app. This licensing model ensures that access to the app's content is restricted to users who have the required permissions.

options.text: If the workspace is in Premium capacity, users without Pro or PPU licenses can view the app content.
options.explanation: When the workspace hosting the Power BI App is moved to Premium capacity, users who do not have Pro or PPU licenses can still view the app content. Premium capacity allows for broader accessibility to the app, enabling users without individual licenses to access the content.

options.text: In Premium capacity, users without Pro or PPU licenses can also copy reports and create new reports from the semantic models.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Within Premium capacity, users who do not have Pro or PPU licenses do not have the capability to copy reports or create new reports from the semantic models. These actions are restricted to users with the appropriate licensing, ensuring data security and integrity.

options.text: Premium capacity allows broader distribution of apps without requiring every user to have a Pro or PPU license.
options.explanation: Premium capacity facilitates wider distribution of apps without mandating that every user holds a Pro or PPU license. This feature allows organizations to share insights and reports more broadly within the company without the need for individual user licenses for every viewer.

options.text: Without Premium capacity, free users can still view the app content.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. In a scenario where the workspace is not in Premium capacity, free users do not have the privilege to view the app content. Access to the app is restricted to users with Power BI Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) licenses, ensuring that only authorized individuals can interact with the app.

explanation: To create or update an app, you need a Power BI Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) license. For app users: If the workspace for this app is not in a Power BI Premium capacity, all users need Power BI Pro or PPU licenses to view the app. If the workspace is in a Power BI Premium capacity (F64 or higher Fabric capacity), users without Pro or PPU licenses can view the app content, but they cannot copy reports or create reports based on the underlying semantic models. Power BI Apps - Licensing Rules Creating or Updating Apps You must have a Power BI Pro license or a Premium Per User (PPU) license. Without Pro/PPU, you cannot publish or update apps. Viewing Apps (App Users) Workspace NOT in Premium capacity Every user who wants to view the app must have Pro or PPU. No exceptions. Standard workspaces require licensed users. Workspace IS in Premium capacity (F64 or higher Fabric capacity) Users without Pro/PPU can still view app content. But they are limited: Cannot copy reports. Cannot create new reports based on the underlying semantic models. They can consume (readonly) dashboards and reports. Keep in Mind Publish = Pro/PPU always View = Pro/PPU unless Premium capacity (P SKU or F64+ Fabric) Premium + free users = View only, no build/copy References: Create a Power BI app - Training | Microsoft Learn

options.text: B. Viewers can only view content, while Contributors can create and edit content

text: What is the primary purpose of applying sensitivity labels in Power BI?

options.text: To ensure compliance with organizational branding guidelines.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Applying sensitivity labels in Power BI is not primarily for ensuring compliance with organizational branding guidelines. Sensitivity labels are used to classify and protect sensitive data, not for branding purposes.

options.text: To classify and protect sensitive data throughout its lifecycle, including when shared externally.
options.explanation: The primary purpose of applying sensitivity labels in Power BI is to classify and protect sensitive data throughout its lifecycle, including when shared externally. This helps ensure that sensitive information is appropriately handled and protected, even when it is being accessed by external parties. Sensitivity labels in Power BI

options.text: To restrict access to Power BI reports based on user roles.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Restricting access to Power BI reports based on user roles is not the primary purpose of applying sensitivity labels. While sensitivity labels can help control access to sensitive data, their main function is to classify and protect data based on its sensitivity level, not user roles.

explanation:
The primary purpose of applying sensitivity labels in Power BI is to classify and protect sensitive data by enforcing consistent security and compliance policies across reports, dashboards, and datasets.

Key Benefits of Sensitivity Labels in Power BI

Data classification

Labels (e.g., Confidential, Highly Confidential, Public) help identify the sensitivity level of the content.

Protection across Microsoft ecosystem

Sensitivity labels applied in Power BI extend to Excel, Office apps, and Microsoft 365 services, ensuring consistent governance.

Automatic policy enforcement

Depending on the label, Power BI can enforce restrictions such as:

Preventing sharing with external users

Applying encryption

Controlling export options (e.g., to Excel, PDF)

Compliance alignment

Helps organizations meet regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, financial regulations) by ensuring sensitive data is handled correctly.

User awareness

Labels make users aware of the sensitivity of the data they are working with, reducing accidental oversharing.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Your company applies a Highly Confidential sensitivity label to a Power BI report in the service. A manager exports the report to Excel and shares it with another team. Which of the following statements correctly describe what happens in this scenario?

options.text: The sensitivity label is visible in the workspace but does not persist when exported.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The sensitivity label applied to a Power BI report persists when the report is exported to Excel, PowerPoint, or PDF. This ensures that the sensitive data remains classified and protected even when shared outside of the Power BI service.

options.text: The sensitivity label persists when exported to Excel, PowerPoint, or PDF.
options.explanation: The protection settings associated with the sensitivity label, such as encryption and access controls, travel with the data when exported outside of Power BI. This helps maintain data security and compliance measures even after the data leaves the Power BI environment.

options.text: The protection settings associated with the label travel with the data outside Power BI.
options.explanation: The sensitivity label plays a crucial role in ensuring compliance and safeguarding data, even when it is exported from Power BI to other formats or shared with external teams. This helps maintain data integrity and confidentiality throughout its lifecycle.

options.text: Exporting removes the sensitivity label, requiring manual reapplication in Excel.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The sensitivity label may be visible in the Power BI workspace where the report is located, but it does not persist when the report is exported to external formats like Excel. This can lead to potential data exposure and security risks if the sensitivity label is not retained.

options.text: The sensitivity label ensures compliance and safeguards data even outside Power BI.
options.explanation: Exporting the report to Excel does not automatically remove the sensitivity label. The label should persist with the data to maintain its classification and protection status, reducing the need for manual re-application of the label in Excel.

explanation:
Even if a manager exports and shares a Power BI file, the sensitivity label can remain attached to the content and may enforce protection depending on how the label is configured in Microsoft Purview. This can include encryption, access restrictions, and usage controls in supported Microsoft 365 applications. However, the level of protection depends on the policies applied to the label.

In short: A sensitivity label such as “Highly Confidential” can travel with the data when it is exported to formats like Excel or PowerPoint, and it can help enforce protection and compliance based on the organization’s security settings.

Keep in Mind:

Definition: Sensitivity labels classify and protect data in Power BI content such as reports, dashboards, and datasets.

Purpose: They help organizations enforce data governance and protect sensitive information across Microsoft 365.

Integration: Sensitivity labels in Power BI are managed through Microsoft Purview Information Protection.

Application Scope: Labels can be applied to datasets, reports, dashboards, and dataflows.

Inheritance: Downstream content (like reports created from labeled datasets) can inherit sensitivity labels.

Propagation: Labels can travel with exported content (for example Excel or PowerPoint), depending on policy configuration.

Manual Application: Users can manually apply labels in Power BI when allowed.

Automatic Application: Administrators can configure auto-labeling based on sensitive data rules.

Visibility: Labels are visible in Power BI Service and Desktop to indicate data sensitivity.

Security Enforcement: Depending on configuration, labels can enforce encryption and access controls when data is exported.

Consistency: Labels help maintain consistent classification across Microsoft 365 applications.

Governance: They support organizational data governance and compliance requirements.

Compliance: Helps meet regulatory standards such as GDPR, HIPAA, and ISO.

Limitations: Labels do not automatically guarantee protection in all scenarios; effectiveness depends on configured policies.

Admin Role: Sensitivity labels and policies are defined in Microsoft Purview, not directly in Power BI.

Exam Focus: Know how labels are applied, inherited, and used to protect data across Power BI and Microsoft 365.

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: A developer applies a Confidential sensitivity label to a .pbix file in Power BI Desktop. Later, they publish the file to the Power BI Service, where the associated semantic model already has a Highly Confidential label. What happens to the sensitivity label in this scenario?

options.text: A. The Desktop label overrides the Service label, so the report remains Confidential.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. In Power BI, when a .pbix file is published to the Power BI Service, the sensitivity label applied in Power BI Desktop can be overridden by the label associated with the semantic model in the Service. Therefore, the report will inherit the label from the Service, not the Desktop.

options.text: B. The Service label overrides the Desktop label, so the report inherits Highly Confidential.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The sensitivity label applied in the Power BI Service takes precedence over the label applied in Power BI Desktop. In this scenario, the report will inherit the Highly Confidential label from the semantic model in the Service, overriding the Confidential label applied in Desktop.

options.text: C. Both labels are applied simultaneously, and users can choose which one to enforce.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. In Power BI, when a .pbix file is published with conflicting sensitivity labels, the most restrictive label is applied to ensure data security and compliance. Users do not have the option to choose which label to enforce; the system automatically applies the most restrictive label.

options.text: D. The most restrictive label between the report and semantic model is applied to the .pbix file.
options.explanation: The correct choice is D because in Power BI, when a .pbix file is published with conflicting sensitivity labels, the system applies the most restrictive label between the report and the semantic model. This ensures that the data is protected according to the highest level of sensitivity set in either the report or the semantic model. Note: When using Download the .pbix in the Power BI service, if the downloaded report and its semantic model have different labels, the more restrictive label will be applied to the .pbix file.

explanation: When sensitivity labels are applied in Power BI, the most restrictive label between the report and the semantic model (dataset) is automatically enforced on the .pbix file. Sensitivity labels can be applied only on dashboards, reports, semantic models, dataflows, and paginated reports. They aren't currently available for workbooks. In Power BI Service: In Power BI Desktop: How it works: If a report has a sensitivity label (e.g., Confidential) and the semantic model has a stricter label (e.g., Highly Confidential), then the .pbix file inherits the Highly Confidential label. This ensures that the highest level of protection is consistently applied, preventing accidental downgrading of sensitivity when exporting or sharing. The applied label travels with the .pbix file, so compliance and protection policies continue outside Power BI. In short: The most restrictive sensitivity label wins, ensuring maximum protection of the data. All about sensitivty labels: Definition: Sensitivity labels classify and protect data in Power BI workspaces. Purpose: They help enforce compliance and protect sensitive information across reports, dashboards, and datasets. Integration: Sensitivity labels in Power BI are integrated with Microsoft Purview Information Protection. Application Scope: Labels can be applied to datasets, reports, dashboards, and dataflows. Inheritance: Content inherits sensitivity labels from parent datasets or reports when published. Propagation: Labels propagate downstream when data is exported to Excel, PDF, or PowerPoint. Manual Application: Analysts can manually apply sensitivity labels to workspace content. Automatic Application: Admins can configure auto-labeling policies for sensitive data. Visibility: Labels are visible in the Power BI service and desktop, ensuring users know data sensitivity. Security Enforcement: Labels enforce encryption and rights management when data is exported. Consistency: Labels ensure consistent classification across Microsoft 365 apps (Excel, Outlook, Teams). Governance: Sensitivity labels support organizational data governance policies. Compliance: They help meet regulatory requirements like GDPR, HIPAA, and ISO standards. User Awareness: Labels raise awareness among users about handling sensitive data responsibly. Limitations: Sensitivity labels don’t restrict access within Power BI itself; they protect data outside Power BI. Export Behavior: When exporting, sensitivity labels ensure files carry the same classification. Workspace Impact: Labels applied in workspaces affect shared content across the organization. Admin Role: Admins define sensitivity labels and policies in Microsoft Purview, not directly in Power BI. Exam Focus: PL-300 expects you to know how to apply, inherit, and propagate labels in Power BI. Best Practice: Always apply the most restrictive label needed to protect sensitive data Youtube Video: Why and how to use data protection in Power BI Keep your data SECURE using Sensitivity Labels // Beginners Guide to Power BI in 2021 104. section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: A company is building a single Power BI Sales Report for all employees across different departments. Employees frequently change departments, and the organization does not want to maintain or update security roles manually whenever these changes happen. The requirement is that each employee should automatically see only the sales data relevant to their current department when they access the report. Which Row-Level Security (RLS) approach should be used?

options.text: A. Static RLS, because roles rarely change.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Static RLS is not the most appropriate method in this scenario because department assignments change frequently. Static RLS would require manual updates every time a department assignment changes, which is not efficient for Tailspin Traders with hundreds of employees.

options.text: B. Dynamic RLS, because roles change frequently and must adapt automatically.
options.explanation: Dynamic RLS is the most appropriate method in this scenario because roles change frequently, and Dynamic RLS can adapt automatically to these changes. It allows each employee to only see sales data for their own department without the need for manual updates whenever department assignments change.

options.text: C. Single SignOn (SSO), because it enforces permissions at the data source level.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Single Sign-On (SSO) is not the most appropriate method in this scenario because it focuses on enforcing permissions at the data source level, rather than restricting access to specific data based on department assignments. SSO is more related to authentication and access control at a broader level.

options.text: D. ObjectLevel Security (OLS), because it restricts access to specific tables and columns.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Object-Level Security (OLS) is not the most appropriate method in this scenario because it restricts access to specific tables and columns, rather than dynamically controlling access based on department assignments. OLS is more suitable for controlling access to specific data objects, not for ensuring each employee only sees sales data for their own department.

explanation: There are several ways to implement RLS in Power BI. The Static method is suitable for a small number of roles that rarely change. The Dynamic method is better for a large number of roles that change frequently. Alternatively, you can use single sign-on (SSO) for some data sources that use Direct Query, enforcing data permissions at the data source level. Additionally, you can use Object-level security (OLS) to restrict access to specific tables and columns like employee salaries or personal information. This method is useful when you need to restrict access to sensitive data at the object level. References: Introduction - Training | Microsoft Learn

section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Tailspin Traders wants to share a combined HR and Sales Report with managers. Managers should see sales data for all departments, but employee salary details must remain hidden from everyone except HR. Which security feature should be applied to achieve this requirement?

options.text: A. RowLevel Security (RLS), because it filters rows based on department.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Row-Level Security (RLS) is used to filter rows based on specific criteria, such as department or user roles. While it can restrict access to certain rows of data, it does not provide the granularity needed to hide specific columns like employee salaries from certain users.

options.text: B. ObjectLevel Security (OLS), because it restricts access to sensitive tables/columns like salaries.
options.explanation: Object-Level Security (OLS) is the correct choice in this scenario because it allows for the restriction of access to specific tables or columns within a dataset. By applying OLS, Tailspin Traders can ensure that only HR has access to sensitive information like employee salaries while still allowing managers to view sales data for all departments.

options.text: C. Static RLS, because salary data rarely changes.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Static RLS is not the ideal choice for this scenario, as it focuses on filtering rows based on static criteria that do not change frequently. In this case, the requirement is to hide sensitive salary details from managers, which may not be effectively achieved through static row-level security.

options.text: D. Dynamic RLS, because employee roles change frequently.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Dynamic RLS is not the best option for this scenario, as it focuses on filtering rows based on changing criteria, such as user roles. While employee roles may change frequently, the requirement is to restrict access to specific columns like salaries, which is better addressed by Object-Level Security (OLS).

explanation:
Why OLS is Used

Restricts access at the object level: OLS allows you to hide specific tables or columns in a semantic model from certain users.

Sensitive data protection: For example, salary information in an HR dataset can be restricted so only authorized users see it.

Complementary to RowLevel Security (RLS):

RLS filters rows of data (e.g., employees only see their department’s records).

OLS hides entire objects (e.g., the Salary column or Compensation table).

Keep in Mind:

HR Analytics dataset contains:

Employee table (Name, Department, Salary)

Performance table (KPIs, Ratings)

With OLS:

General managers may see Name and Department but not Salary.

HR leadership can see all columns, including Salary.

text: Tailspin Traders wants to implement RowLevel Security (RLS) in Power BI Desktop so that each department only sees its own sales data. You are asked to arrange the steps in the correct order. A. Create a role for each department on the Manage security roles page. B. Add a filter or DAX expression to the role (e.g., [Department] = "Game"). C. Select the Modeling tab and choose Manage Roles.

options.text: C - A - B
options.explanation: Selecting the Modeling tab and choosing Manage Roles is the first step in creating RLS roles in Power BI Desktop. This is where you can define and manage roles for your data model.

options.text: A - B - C
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. After selecting the Modeling tab and choosing Manage Roles, the next step is to create a role for each department on the Manage security roles page. This is where you can define the specific access restrictions for each department.

options.text: B - C - A
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Once you have created a role for each department on the Manage security roles page, the final step is to add a filter or DAX expression to the role. This filter or expression will define the criteria for which data each department can access, ensuring that they only see their own sales data.

explanation: Step 1: Select Modeling tab - Manage Roles Step 2: Create a role for each department Step 3: Add a filter or DAX expression to the role Create RLS roles in Power BI Desktop Power BI row-level security (RLS) uses DAX to control who can see which data. Consider it as always adding another filter to the appropriate users, regardless of the filters, slicers, or interactions that the users choose on a Power BI report. To create RLS roles in Power BI Desktop, select the Modeling tab, and then select Manage Roles. On the Manage security roles page, create a role for each department, and then add a filter or DAX expression to it. For instance, you can create a role called Game and then add the filter or DAX expression [Department] = "Game". Then, whenever a member of that role interacts with the report, Power BI will add that filter to their interactions, thus limiting what they see. A fixed value is used in the filter on the right side of the equal sign (in this case, "Game"). The intention is that, if you ever need to add a category, you will need to create a new role with a new value in the DAX expression. The DAX filter is applied to every interaction, slicer, and filter that the user applies. If you have a DAX filter that performs poorly, the user experience will be negatively impacted. Therefore, keep the DAX filter as simple as possible. References: Configure row-level security with the static method - Training | Microsoft Learn

explanation: You can test Row-Level Security (RLS) roles in Power BI Desktop using the Modeling tab and the View as roles option. In the View as roles window, select the Game role. section: Design effective reports in Power BI
text: Tailspin Traders wants to implement dynamic RLS so that each employee only sees their own sales records. The company maintains an Employees table with email addresses and a relationship to the Sales table. Which DAX function should be used in the RLS filter to ensure that when Russel King signs in with russel@tailwindtraders.com, he only sees his four sales?

options.text: A. USERNAME() - Returns the authenticated user as a text value.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The USERNAME() function returns the authenticated user as a text value, but it does not compare this value with the Employees table to implement dynamic RLS based on the user's email address. Be aware that the USERNAME function returns the user in the format of DOMAIN\username when used in Power BI Desktop. However, when used in the Power BI service, it returns the format of the user's User Principal Name (UPN), like username@adventureworks.com. Because of this difference, many models prefer using USERPRINCIPALNAME() for consistency in the Power BI Service.

options.text: B. USERPRINCIPALNAME() - Compares the signedin user’s email with the Employees table.
options.explanation: The USERPRINCIPALNAME() function is the correct choice for implementing dynamic RLS in this scenario. It allows for comparing the signed-in user's email with the Employees table to ensure that each employee only sees their own sales records.

options.text: C. CUSTOMDATA() - Returns the CustomData property passed in the connection string.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The CUSTOMDATA() function returns the CustomData property passed in the connection string, which is not relevant for implementing dynamic RLS based on the user's email address and ensuring that each employee only sees their own sales records.

options.text: D. A fixed string filter, e.g., [Department] = "Game".
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Using a fixed string filter, such as [Department] = "Game", is not suitable for implementing dynamic RLS based on the user's email address. It does not provide the necessary functionality to restrict access to specific sales records for each employee.

explanation: USERNAME or USERPRINCIPALNAME - Returns the Power BI authenticated user as a text value. CUSTOMDATA - Returns the CustomData property passed in the connection string. Non-Power BI reporting tools that connect to the dataset by using a connection string can set this property, like Microsoft Excel. Keep in Mind: Be aware that the USERNAME function returns the user in the format of DOMAIN\username when used in Power BI Desktop. However, when used in the Power BI service, it returns the format of the user's User Principal Name (UPN), like username@adventureworks.com. Alternatively, you can use the USERPRINCIPALNAME function, which always returns the user in the user principal name format. References: Configure row-level security with the dynamic method - Training | Microsoft Learn

explanation:
Here’s the correct order of steps to successfully add members to the Game role in Power BI Service:

A. Find the semantic model with the same name as your report. (Locate the dataset/semantic model that powers the report.)

B. Select the ellipsis (…) button and then choose Security. (Open the security settings for that semantic model.)

text: Rupali is a data modeler at Adventure Works who is developing an import model to analyze employee timesheet data. The employee table stores the employee social security number (SSN) in a column. While the model will be available for all company managers, it will also be available to employees in the Payroll department. However, reports must only reveal employee SSNs to payroll employees. What feature should Rupali use to restrict access to the SSN column?

options.text: RLS
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. RLS (Row-Level Security) is used to restrict access to rows of data based on the user's identity. It is not the appropriate feature for restricting access to a specific column like the employee SSN in this scenario.

options.text: SSO
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. SSO (Single Sign-On) is a method that allows users to access multiple applications with one set of login credentials. It is not related to restricting access to specific columns in a data model.

options.text: OLS
options.explanation: OLS (Object-Level Security) is the feature that should be used to restrict access to the SSN column in this scenario. OLS allows for the restriction of access to specific objects, such as columns, based on user roles or permissions. In this case, OLS can be used to ensure that only payroll employees have access to view the employee SSN column in the reports.

explanation: You can use OLS (object-level security) to secure the SSN column in the employee table. Object-level security (OLS) enables model authors to secure specific tables or columns from report viewers. For example, a column that includes personal data can be restricted so that only certain viewers can see and interact with it. In addition, you can also restrict object names and metadata. This added layer of security prevents users without the appropriate access levels from discovering business-critical or sensitive personal information like employee or financial records. For viewers that don’t have the required permission, it's as if the secured tables or columns don't exist. Keep in Mind: Like row-level security (RLS), OLS is also defined within model roles. Currently, you can't create OLS definitions natively in Power BI Desktop. To create roles on Power BI Desktop semantic models, use external tools such as Tabular Editor. text: Where can you test RLS by using different security roles?

options.text: Power BI Desktop only
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Testing RLS by using different security roles can be done in Power BI Desktop, but this limits the testing to a local environment and does not allow for testing in the Power BI service where the reports will be shared and accessed by others.

options.text: Power BI service only
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Testing RLS in the Power BI service only may not provide a complete testing environment as it does not allow for testing and validation of RLS implementation during the development phase in Power BI Desktop before publishing the reports to the service.

options.text: Both Power BI Desktop and Power BI service
options.explanation:
Testing RLS by using different security roles in both Power BI Desktop and Power BI service is the most comprehensive approach. It allows for testing and validation of RLS implementation during development in Power BI Desktop and ensures that the security roles work as intended when the reports are shared and accessed in the Power BI service.
Checking out the new Power BI RLS Editor
Row-Level Security in Power BI (Part 3): Assign Roles and Test in Power BI Service

explanation: How to Test RLS in Each Environment: Power BI Desktop After defining RLS roles in Modeling > Manage Roles, you can test them locally. Use Modeling > View as Roles to simulate how the report looks for users assigned to specific roles. This lets you confirm filters are applied correctly before publishing. Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn Row Level Security (RLS) In Power BI With Examples Power BI Service Once the report is published, go to the semantic model (dataset) settings in the workspace. Under Security, you can assign Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) users or groups to roles. Use the Test as role option to validate how the report behaves for those users in the Service. Keep in Mind: Desktop = designtime testing (before publishing). Service = deploymenttime testing (with actual users/groups). Together, they ensure RLS is correctly applied and enforced across both development and production environments. In short: You can test RLS in Power BI Desktop (View as Roles) and in the Power BI Service (Test as role).

Example: What were the average sales amount by category? Pre-populated suggestion tiles: Questions to help users consider how to phrase their questions. text: Scenario: You are analyzing sales data in Power BI Service using Quick Insights. You notice a card showing a sudden spike in revenue for a specific region. You want to drill deeper into this card to uncover related trends without rerunning insights across the entire dataset. Which action should you take?

options.text: A. Select Get insights from the card to generate scoped insights.
options.explanation: Selecting "Get insights from the card" allows you to generate scoped insights specifically related to the data displayed on the card. This action helps you drill deeper into the sudden spike in revenue for the specific region without rerunning insights across the entire dataset, providing more focused analysis.

options.text: B. Pin the card to a dashboard and configure alerts for deeper analysis.
options.explanation: Pinning the card to a dashboard and configuring alerts may help in monitoring the sudden spike in revenue, but it does not directly address the need to drill deeper into the card to uncover related trends without rerunning insights across the entire dataset. This action focuses more on dashboard visualization and alerting rather than detailed analysis.

options.text: C. Open the card in Focus mode and apply filters to explore related trends.
options.explanation: Opening the card in Focus mode and applying filters to explore related trends can help in analyzing the sudden spike in revenue for the specific region, but it does not provide the option to generate scoped insights without rerunning insights across the entire dataset. This action allows for more detailed exploration but may not be as efficient as selecting "Get insights from the card."

explanation:
Scoped analysis: Instead of scanning the entire dataset, Power BI narrows its analysis to the measure or value shown in the card (e.g., Revenue for Region A).

Efficiency: Saves time by avoiding a full dataset rescan.

Contextual insights: Helps you quickly understand anomalies like a sudden spike in revenue for a particular region.

Actionable exploration: You can drill deeper into the reasons behind the change without leaving the context of that card.

For example,

You have a Revenue card showing ₹50M for the South Region.

Selecting Get insights from the card might reveal:

A sudden increase due to a new product launch.

A seasonal sales surge.

A large order from a single customer.

In short: Get insights from the card provides focused, contextual explanations for the value in that card, helping you drill deeper into anomalies without rerunning insights across the entire dataset.

explanation: Live tiles: When you pin an entire report page as a live tile, the tile on the dashboard remains interactive and reflects changes made in the report (including slicer selections, filters, and visuals). Static tiles: If you pin individual visuals (like charts or tables), those tiles are static snapshots and do not update dynamically when slicers are changed. They only refresh when the dataset refreshes. Realtime interactivity: By pinning the whole report page, the manager can interact with slicers directly on the dashboard tile, and the tile will update in realtime. The manager wants a dashboard tile that updates immediately when slicers are changed. Then pinning the entire report page as a live tile ensures the dashboard behaves like the report itself, maintaining interactivity.

explanation:
Security roles in Power BI are defined in Power BI Desktop and then published to the Service. - True

You create roles in Power BI Desktop under Modeling > Manage Roles.

RowLevel Security (RLS) restricts data access for specific users based on filters you set. - True

RLS applies filters at the row level of a dataset.

Example: In an HR dataset, you can filter so that employees only see data for their own department.

This ensures personalized and secure views of the same dataset without duplicating reports.

Security roles can only be applied at the workspace level, not at the dataset level. - False

Security roles are applied at the dataset (semantic model) level, not at the workspace level.

text: Your organization has multiple workspaces in Power BI Service. Different teams (Finance, HR, Sales) all need to use the same cleaned customer data. You want to avoid duplicating ETL steps in each dataset. Which Power BI Service feature should you use?

options.text: A. Datasets - to store the cleaned data model and refresh it for each workspace.

options.text: C. Dataflows - to create reusable ETL pipelines that prepare data across workspaces.
options.explanation: Dataflows in Power BI Service are specifically designed to create reusable ETL pipelines that prepare data across workspaces. By using dataflows, you can avoid duplicating ETL steps in each dataset and instead create a single pipeline that all teams can connect to and use the same cleaned customer data. explanation:
Tips:

Datasets hold the model but don’t provide reusable ETL across workspaces.

Reports are for visualization, not data prep.

Apps distribute content, not transform data.

Dataflows are the only feature designed for reusable ETL pipelines across workspaces.

Key Features of Dataflows

ETL Capabilities: Dataflows allow users to perform ETL operations, making it easier to prepare data for analysis and reporting.

Centralized Data Management: By storing data in Azure Data Lake, dataflows provide a single source of truth, enhancing data governance and consistency.

Scheduled Refresh: Users can set up automatic data refresh schedules, ensuring that reports and dashboards always reflect the latest data.

Reusability: Dataflows can be reused across different reports, reducing redundancy in data preparation efforts.

explanation: Steps to Create a Subscription and Add Users Open the dashboard in Power BI Service Navigate to the workspace and open the dashboard that contains your KPI visual. Select the Subscribe option At the top of the dashboard, click on Subscribe (bell icon). This opens the subscription pane. Create a new subscription Choose Add new subscription. Give the subscription a descriptive name (e.g., Revenue KPI Daily Update). Choose the content to include Select the KPI visual or the entire dashboard tile you want to send in the subscription email. Set the schedule Configure the subscription to run daily at the desired time (e.g., 8:00 AM). This ensures the five users get the latest KPI value each morning. Add recipients Enter the email addresses of the five specific users. You can add individual Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) users or security groups. Save the subscription Once saved, Power BI will automatically send the KPI updates to those users according to the schedule. Email subscriptions for reports and dashboards in the Power BI service - Power BI | Microsoft Learn Keep in Mind: Subscriptions are managed in the Power BI Service, not in Desktop. Users receive an email with the KPI visual snapshot at the scheduled time. If the dataset refreshes before the subscription runs, the email will include the latest data. You can edit or remove recipients anytime by going back to the subscription settings.

explanation:
Direct Connection to Azure SQL Database

Power BI Service can connect directly to Azure SQL Database without requiring an onpremises data gateway.

This is because Azure SQL Database is a cloudbased service, and Power BI Service can establish a secure connection over the internet.

Authentication is handled using Azure Active Directory (Microsoft Entra ID) or SQL authentication, depending on how the database is configured.

When a Gateway is Required

The onpremises data gateway is needed only when connecting to onpremises data sources, such as:

SQL Server hosted in your local datacenter

Oracle, SAP HANA, Teradata, or other onprem databases

Filebased sources like Excel or CSV stored on local servers

In these cases, the gateway acts as a bridge between Power BI Service (cloud) and your onprem environment.

Scenario 2 (OnPrem): Connecting Power BI Service to SQL Server in your datacenter - Gateway required.

options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The user included in the groups for "Florida" and "2022" should have access to all data related to Florida and all data from the year 2022. options.text: All data from Florida and all data from 2022.
options.explanation: Given that the user is part of the groups for "Florida" and "2022", they should be able to see all data from Florida and all data from the year 2022 in the related report. options.text: Only the data that is related to Florida from the year 2022.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. With the user being included in the groups for "Florida" and "2022", they should have visibility into all data related to Florida and all data from the year 2022. The row-level security measures based on state and year should grant the user access to the relevant information without restricting their view to only specific subsets.

options.text: All data from all states and all years.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The user included in the groups for "Florida" and "2022" should not receive an error message and should be able to see all data from Florida and all data from the year 2022 in the related report. The row-level security settings should allow the user to view the data corresponding to the specified state and year without limitations.

explanation: Role 1: State = Florida - grants access to all rows where the state is Florida (across all years). Role 2: Year = 2022 - grants access to all rows where the year is 2022 (across all states). Because the user is in both groups, the filters combine as: (State=Florida) OR (Year=2022) The user will see: All data for Florida (regardless of year). All data for 2022 (regardless of state). So the user’s view is broader than just Florida in 2022 - they get the union of both conditions. Keep in Mind: When a user belongs to multiple roles/groups, Power BI applies the filters using OR logic, not AND. This means the user will see all rows that satisfy any of the role conditions. options.text: In Power BI Premium, you can schedule up to 48 dataset refreshes per day. - True In Power BI Pro (shared capacity), you can schedule up to 8 dataset refreshes per day. - True The maximum dataset size in Power BI Pro is 1 GB, while Premium supports much larger datasets (up to 400 GB with large models). - False Exporting summarized data from Power BI Service to Excel is limited to 150,000 rows. - False A dashboard can be shared with a maximum of 100 users or groups per share action. - True A single report can't have more than 1,000 sharing links. - False
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. The dataset size limit, the Excel export row limit, and the sharing-links limit are all real, documented figures - flagging them False makes this option inaccurate.

options.text: In Power BI Premium, you can schedule up to 48 dataset refreshes per day. - True In Power BI Pro (shared capacity), you can schedule up to 8 dataset refreshes per day. - True The maximum dataset size in Power BI Pro is 1 GB, while Premium supports much larger datasets (up to 400 GB with large models). - True Exporting summarized data from Power BI Service to Excel is limited to 150,000 rows. - True A dashboard can be shared with a maximum of 100 users or groups per share action. - True A single report can't have more than 1,000 sharing links. - True
options.explanation: This is the correct option - all six statements are accurate per current Microsoft documentation.

explanation: Dataset Refresh Limits Power BI Premium - 48 refreshes/day Premium capacity allows scheduling up to 48 dataset refreshes per day (about every 30 minutes), ideal for scenarios like finance or operations where data changes frequently. Power BI Pro (shared capacity) - 8 refreshes/day In Pro, you can schedule up to 8 refreshes per day. Manual, UI-triggered on-demand refreshes don't count toward this limit. Dataset Size Limits Power BI Pro - 1 GB per dataset. Power BI Premium - up to 400 GB with large models, enabling enterprise-scale analytics with much larger datasets. Export Limits Exporting summarized data from Power BI Service to Excel is limited to 150,000 rows. For larger exports, users typically rely on Paginated Reports or direct queries. Sharing Limits When you share a dashboard directly, the share dialog supports up to 100 separate users or groups per share action (not 500 - that's a common misconception). To reach a bigger audience, use a security group or publish an app from the workspace. Separately, a single report can't have more than 1,000 sharing links; once you hit that limit, remove links for "Specific people" and grant those users direct access instead. text: To sync slicers, they need to contain the same fields. True or false?

options.text: True
options.explanation: True. In order to sync slicers in Power BI, they must contain the same fields. This ensures that the slicers are connected and can filter the data in a synchronized manner across different visuals in the report. Sync and use slicers on other pages - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: False
options.explanation: The statement is incorrect. Slicers in Power BI need to contain the same fields in order to sync them and have consistent filtering across visuals. If the slicers have different fields, they cannot be synced effectively.

explanation:
Why Slicers Must Use the Same Field

Consistency of filtering logic

When slicers are synced, Power BI applies the same filter across multiple report pages or visuals.

If slicers are based on different fields, the filter context would not align, and synchronization would fail.

Shared filter context

For example, if you have a slicer on “Region”, syncing works only if all slicers are tied to the Region field in the model.

If one slicer uses “Country” and another uses “Region”, they cannot sync because they represent different fields.

For example,

You create a slicer for Year on Page 1.

You create another slicer for Year on Page 2.

By syncing slicers, when you select 2022 on Page 1, Page 2 automatically filters to 2022 as well.

If instead Page 2 had a slicer for Quarter, syncing would not be possible because the fields differ.

Keep in Mind:

How to Sync Slicers:

* Add slicers based on the same field across report pages. * Go to the View tab - Sync Slicers pane. * Select which pages the slicer should sync with. * Choose whether the slicer should be visible or hidden on each page.

text: Which of the following features we get when pinning a live report page in our dashboard?

options.text: Visuals on your dashboards reflect changes live.
options.explanation: When pinning a live report page in a dashboard, the visuals on the dashboard reflect changes in real-time. This means that any updates or modifications made to the underlying report will be immediately reflected on the pinned page within the dashboard. Pin an entire report page to a Power BI dashboard - Power BI | Microsoft Learn

options.text: Enables data streaming.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Pinning a live report page in a dashboard does not specifically enable data streaming. Data streaming is a separate feature that allows for real-time data updates and visualization, but it is not directly related to pinning a report page in a dashboard.

options.text: Enables using data alerts.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Pinning a live report page in a dashboard does not enable the use of data alerts. Data alerts are a separate feature in Power BI that allows users to set up notifications based on specific data conditions or thresholds, but it is not directly related to pinning report pages in dashboards.

options.text: Visuals can be adjusted live and directly through the dashboard.
options.explanation: This is incorrect option. Users can interact with a pinned live report page directly on the dashboard, such as clicking a bar to cross-filter or cross-highlight the other visuals on the tile. However, you cannot adjust or reconfigure the visuals themselves (change chart type, fields, formatting) from the dashboard. Those changes must be made back in the original report, and they then appear on the dashboard tile automatically.

explanation:
What Happens When You Pin a Live Report Page:

Live connection to the report

When you pin an entire report page as a live tile to a dashboard, the tile remains connected to the underlying report.

Any changes made to the report (filters, slicers, new visuals, formatting updates) are immediately reflected on the dashboard tile.

Realtime interactivity

Users can interact with slicers and filters directly on the dashboard tile.

This makes the dashboard behave almost like the report itself, offering dynamic updates rather than static snapshots.

Automatic updates

If the dataset refreshes or the report is modified, the dashboard tile updates automatically without needing to repin.

This ensures the dashboard always shows the latest data and design.

Difference from Pinning Individual Visuals

Pinned visuals (static tiles)

If you pin a single chart, KPI, or table, it becomes a static snapshot.

It only updates when the dataset refreshes, and it does not respond to slicer changes or report edits.

Pinned report page (live tile)

Reflects realtime changes in filters, slicers, and visuals.

Provides a more interactive experience directly on the dashboard.
